Machine Reading at Scale (MRS) involves a system processing a query to extract precise output from a large knowledge base. This task combines information retrieval (IR) and machine comprehension (MC). While representation learning has advanced IR and MC separately, few studies explore their relationship and combined design for MRS. This work proposes a simple pipeline system with hierarchical semantic retrieval at paragraph and sentence levels, evaluating its impact on downstream tasks. The system achieved state-of-the-art results on FEVER and HOTPOTQA fact verification and open-domain multi-hop QA leaderboards. Ablation and analysis studies quantify the contribution of neural retrieval modules, demonstrating their importance in filtering information, saving computation, shaping upstream data distribution, and providing better data for downstream modeling.

Extracting external textual knowledge for machine comprehension systems is a challenging problem. Success requires precise retrieval of relevant information from a large knowledge source and deep understanding of both the selected knowledge and the input query. The MRS task, as defined by Chen et al. (2017), requires semantic retrieval and comprehension at different granularities for the final downstream task.

Progress in MRS has been driven by improvements in individual IR or comprehension sub-modules, leveraging advancements in representative learning. However, evaluations have primarily focused on the final downstream task, with less emphasis on intermediate retrieval performance, partly due to a lack of annotated data for intermediate retrieval in an MRS setting. This has led to a convention where upstream retrieval modules prioritize coverage for downstream tasks rather than exact information retrieval. This approach is misaligned with the MRS objective, which emphasizes joint performance and optimizing the relationship between semantic retrieval and downstream comprehension.

To highlight the importance of semantic retrieval for downstream comprehension, a hierarchical pipeline system for MRS is established using Wikipedia as the knowledge source. The system comprises a term-based retrieval module, neural modules for paragraph-level and sentence-level retrieval, and a downstream task module. The system was evaluated on FEVER and HOTPOTQA, large-scale open-domain benchmarks for fact verification and multi-hop QA, where intermediate annotation of evidences allows for accurate retrieval performance evaluation. The system achieved state-of-the-art results: 45.32% answer EM and 25.14% joint EM on HOTPOTQA (an 8% absolute improvement in answer EM and doubling the joint EM over previous best results), and 67.26% on FEVER score (a 3% absolute improvement over previously published systems).

Empirical studies validate design decisions, proving the necessity of both paragraph-level and sentence-level retrieval for maintaining good performance. These studies further illustrate that improved semantic retrieval modules not only enhance recall and the upper bound of the downstream task but also play a crucial role in shaping the downstream data distribution, providing more relevant and high-quality data for downstream sub-module training and inference.

B Term-Based Retrieval Details

FEVER: We used the same key-word matching method in Nie et al. (2019) to get a candidate set for each query. We also used TF-IDF (Chen et al., 2017) method to get top-5 related documents for each query. Then, the two sets were combined to get the final term-based retrieval set for FEVER. The mean and standard deviation of the number of retrieved paragraphs in the merged set were 8.06 and 4.88.

HOTPOTQA: We first used the same procedure on FEVER to get an initial candidate set for each query in HOTPOTQA. Because HOTPOTQA requires at least 2-hop reasoning for each query, we extract all hyperlinked documents from the retrieved documents in the initial candidate set, rank them with TF-IDF (Chen et al., 2017) score, and then select top-5 most related documents and add them to the candidate set. This gives the final term-based retrieval set for HOTPOTQA. The mean and standard deviation of the number of retrieved paragraphs for each query in HOTPOTQA were 39.43 and 16.05.

Related work includes Neural Query Language (NQL), which defines differentiable templates for multi-step access to a symbolic Knowledge Base (KB) with explicitly enumerated relations. The focus here is on implicit relations derived from text mention representations. Knowledge Graph embeddings attach continuous representations to discrete symbols for use in deep networks, allowing generalization to unseen facts. However, text corpora are more complete in their information content.

Talmor & Berant (2018) also explored answering compositional questions by treating a text corpus as a KB. Their approach involves parsing the query into a computation tree and running a black-box QA model on its leaves independently, which prevents end-to-end training. Recent work on complex QA utilizes graph neural networks or identifies entity paths in text, relying on a small pool of relevant evidence documents for multi-step QA. Some approaches incorporate dynamic retrieval to add text about relevant entities identified in previous model layers. This query-dependent processing of evidence text leads to slower inference speeds compared to pre-processed indexed representations. Methods performing multi-step retrieval interleaved with a reading comprehension model share this limitation.

DrKIT is a differentiable module capable of answering multi-hop questions directly using an entity-linked text corpus. It emulates KB traversal over the text corpus, enabling the following of relations in a "virtual" KB over text. DrKIT achieves state-of-the-art results on the MetaQA dataset for natural language question answering, with a 9-point increase in the 3-hop case. An efficient implementation using sparse operations and inner product search provides a 10-100x increase in Queries/sec over baseline approaches.

The Wikipedia abstracts released by Yang et al. (2018) were used as the text corpus. The total number of entities, 5.23 million, equals the number of abstracts. Hyperlinks in the text are considered mentions of the entities to which they point, resulting in 22.8 million total mentions in a 34GB index. For pretraining mention representations, a comparison was made between using the WikiData KB and directly using the HotpotQA training questions with TFIDF-based retrieved passages as negative examples. AE-M[e, m] is set to 1 if entity e is mentioned on the page of entity m, or vice versa. For entity linking over questions, the top 20 entities are retrieved based on the match between a bigram-based TFIDF vector of the question and a similar vector derived from the entity's surface form (the Wiki article title). The gold entities required for retrieval were found within 2 hops of the entities linked in this manner for 87% of the development examples.

Unlike MetaQA and WikiData, the number of hops required for each HotpotQA question is unknown in advance. Therefore, DrKIT was run for 2 hops per question. A weighted average of the distribution over entities after each hop was taken: Z* = p0Z0 + p1Z1 + p2Z2. Z0 consists of entities linked to the question itself, rescored based on an encoding of the question, as some required entities may be in this set. Z1 and Z2 are given by Eq. 4. The mixing weights pi are the softmax outputs of a classifier on top of another question encoding, trained end-to-end on the retrieval task. This process can be viewed as a soft mixing of different templates, ranging from 0 to 2 hops, for answering a question, similar to NQL (Cohen et al., 2019).

Retrieval results were compared to those presented in Das et al. (2019b). Accuracy @k retrievals, the fraction of questions for which both required passages are in the top k retrieved ones, was measured. An improvement in accuracy was observed across the board, with higher gains at @2 and @5. The main baseline is an entity-centric IR approach that uses a BERT-based re-ranker on 200 passage pairs per question. DrKIT also shows over a 10x improvement in queries per second during inference. Inference time was measured with a batch size of 1 for both models for fair comparison. DrKIT can be run with batch sizes up to 40, while the entity-centric IR baseline cannot due to the high number of BERT runs per query. When comparing different datasets for pretraining the index, there was not much difference between using the WikiData KB or the HotpotQA questions. The latter yielded better accuracy @2, but the best overall performance was achieved using a combination of both.

The performance of the baseline reading comprehension model from Yang et al. (2018) was evaluated with passages retrieved by DrKIT. A significant improvement was seen over the baseline using TFIDF-based retrieval, but only a small improvement over passages retrieved by the entity-centric IR baseline, despite DrKIT's improved accuracy @10. Among the 33% of questions where the top 10 passages did not contain both correct passages, the passage containing the answer was missing for approximately 20%.

Embeddings are 400-dimensional for mentions and queries, and 200-dimensional for start and end positions. The index size is 750MB. When computing AE-M, the entity to mention co-occurrence matrix, only mentions in the top 50 paragraphs matched with an entity are retained for sparsity. Single-hop questions and relation extraction:
A dataset of 1M slot-filling queries of the form (e1, R, ?) paired with Wikipedia sentences mentioning e1 was used for training systems answering single-step slot-filling questions from candidate passages. For an open version of this task, answers are extracted from a corpus. This corpus is constructed by collecting and entity-linking all paragraphs in Wikipedia articles of 8K subject entities in the dev and test sets, resulting in 109K passages. After constructing TFIDF AE-M and coreference BM-E matrices for this corpus, the pre-trained index is used to answer test set queries. Figure 4 (Right) shows Hits@1 performance on the Levy et al. (2017) slot-filling dataset, with results reported for all relations, a 'Rare' subset (relations with frequencies < 5 in training data), and a 'Frequent' subset. DrKIT on entity-mentions outperforms other phrase-based models, demonstrating the benefit of indexing only entity-mentions in single-hop questions over all spans. DrKit-entities shows high Hits@1 performance on the Rare relations subset, indicating generalization to less frequent data due to natural language representations of entities and relations.

Probing Experiments:
To compare representations learned by a BERT model fine-tuned on the WikiData slot-filling task, two probing experiments were designed. In each, BERT model parameters (mention encoders) were fixed, and only query encoders were trained. A weighted average of BERT layers was used, with weights learned on the probing task.

Experiment 1: Train and test on shared-entity negatives. Good performance indicates the BERT model reliably encodes fine-grained entity-type information. BERT performs well, suggesting it encodes fine-grained types well.

Experiment 2: Train and test on shared-relation negatives. Good performance indicates the BERT model reliably encodes entity co-occurrence information. A large performance drop for BERT suggests it does not encode entity co-occurrence information well. DrKIT's good performance on both experiments suggests fine-tuning on slot-filling primarily helps contextual representations to encode entity co-occurrence information in addition to entity type information.

On HotpotQA, DrKIT identifies top passages likely to contain the answer. A separate BERT-based model, adapted from SQuAD, extracts the answer from a concatenation of these passages. For boolean questions, a 3-way classifier on the [CLS] representation determines if the answer is a "span", "yes", or "no". If "span" is predicted, start and end positions are extracted; otherwise, the answer is "yes" or "no". For supporting fact prediction, each sentence in the concatenated passages is prepended with [unused0]. A binary classifier on the representation of each [unused0] predicts 1 for supporting facts and 0 for non-supporting facts. During inference, sentences with a classifier output probability > 0.5 are considered supporting facts. The training loss is the average of losses for the 3-way classifier (Lcls), supporting fact classifiers (Lsp), and span start/end positions (Lst, Len): L = (Lcls + Lsp + Lst + Len)/4.

The system is trained on 5 passages per question from HotpotQA's distractor setting: 2 gold and 3 negative passages from a TFIDF retriever. Gold passages are placed first in 60% of examples; the rest are randomly shuffled. Hyperparameters include batch size 32, learning rate 5 x 10-5, 5 training epochs, and a maximum combined passage length of 512.

Filling data improves performance considerably, but DrKIT trained on the same data improves on it. A large improvement over cascaded architectures is seen with end-to-end training, made possible by the differentiable operation introduced. DrKIT performance trained against an index of fixed BERT-large mention representations is comparable to the re-trained version of PIQA but lags behind DrKIT pre-trained using the KB, highlighting the importance of the scheme outlined in SS2.3. Runtime gains of 2x-3x to DrKIT are observed due to the efficient implementation of entity-mention expansion of SS2.2.

Analysis:
Experiments on the dataset of slot-filling queries released by Levy et al. (2017) were conducted to understand accuracy gains for DrKIT. An open version of the task was constructed by collecting Wikipedia articles of all subject entities. PIQA trained on SQuAD achieves 30% macro-avg accuracy, improving to 46% when re-trained on slot-filling data. A version of DrKIT selecting from all spans in the corpus performs similarly to PIQA (50%), but using entity linking significantly improves to 66%. It achieves 55% accuracy answering queries about rare relations (observed < 5 times in training data). Probing experiments comparing representations learned using slot-filling to vanilla BERT found them comparable in detecting fine-grained entity types, but the slot-filling version is significantly better at encoding entity co-occurrence information.

Dataset:
HotpotQA is a dataset of over 100K crowd-sourced multi-hop questions and answers over introductory Wikipedia passages. The open-domain full-wiki setting is used where the two gold passages required to answer the question are not known in advance. Answers are free-form text spans. We view Zt-1, Zt as weighted multisets of entities, and st(m, z, q) as implicitly selecting mentions that correspond to a relation R. Equation 4 becomes a differentiable implementation of Zt = Zt-1.follow(R), mimicking graph traversal in a traditional KB. We call Equation 4 a textual follow operation.

**Training and Inference**
The model is trained end-to-end by optimizing the cross-entropy loss between ZT, the weighted set of entities after T hops, and the ground truth answer set A. A temperature coefficient l is used when computing the softmax in Equation 4 to prevent overly peaked distributions of Zt due to high inner product scores of top-K retrieved mentions. Taking the maximum over the mention set of an entity Mzt in Equation 2 works better than taking a sum, optimizing only over the most confident mention of each entity for corpora like Wikipedia with low redundancy.

**Efficient Implementation**

**Sparse TFIDF Mention Encoding**
To compute the sparse-matrix AE-M for entity-mention expansion in Equation 4, TFIDF vectors F(m) and G(zt-1) are constructed over unigrams and bigrams, hashed to a vocabulary of 16M buckets. F computes the vector from the passage around m, while G uses only the surface form of zt-1. This retrieves all mentions in a document using zt-1 as a query. The number of retrieved mentions per entity is limited to a maximum of u, resulting in a |E| x |M| sparse-matrix.

**Efficient Entity-Mention Expansion**
The expansion from a set of entities to mentions occurring around them is computed using a sparse-matrix by sparse-vector product ZT t-1AE-M. A lower bound for multiplying a sparse |E| x |M| matrix (with maximum u non-zeros per row) by a sparse |E| x 1 vector (with K non-zeros) is ohm(Ku). This bound is independent of the size of AE-M. To achieve this, a vector-driven multiplication algorithm is used. Relevant rows are sliced from AE-M. This is enabled by representing AE-M as two row-wise lists of variable-sized lists of indices and values of non-zero elements, creating a "ragged" representation. This representation allows slicing corresponding to non-zero entries in the vector in O(log |E|) time. The resulting K sparse-vectors, each with at most u non-zero elements, are added, weighted by corresponding values from ZT t-1, in O(K max{K, u}) time. This implementation is feasible with deep learning frameworks like TensorFlow.

**Efficient Top-K Mention Relevance Filtering**
To make the computation of Equation 4 feasible, an efficient method is needed to get top-K relevant mentions related to an entity in zt-1 for a question q, without enumerating all possibilities. By restricting the scoring function st(m, zt-1, q) to an inner product, a parallel approximation across all mentions m is possible. Let f(m) be a dense encoding of m, and gt(q, zt-1) be a dense encoding of the question q for the t-th hop. The scoring function becomes st(m, zt-1, q)  exp {f(m) * gt(q, zt-1)}. This can be computed in parallel by multiplying a matrix f(M) = [f(m1); f(m2); . . .] with gt(q, zt-1). For large matrices, an approximate algorithm for Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) is used to find the K top-scoring elements. The complexity of this filtering step using MIPS is roughly O(Kp polylog|M|).

**Mention and Question Encoders**
Mentions are encoded by passing the passages they are con-

Mention and Question Encoders. Mentions are encoded by passing their containing passages through a BERT-large model. For a mention $m$ in passage $d$ from position $i$ to $j$, its encoding is $f(m) = W^T [H_d^i; H_d^j]$, where $H_d$ is the BERT output sequence and $W$ is a linear projection to size $p$. Queries are encoded with a smaller BERT-like model. They are tokenized with WordPieces, prepended with a [CLS] token, and passed through a 4-layer Transformer network, producing an output sequence $H_q$. For each hop $t = 1, \dots, T$, two additional Transformer layers are added to $H_q$. The first produces a MIPS query $H_q^{st}$ for a start token, and the second produces $H_q^{en}$ for an end token. The combined query is $\tilde{g}_t(q) = V^T [H_q^{st}; H_q^{en}]$. To condition on progress, embeddings of $z_{t-1}$ are added. Entity embeddings $E \in \mathbb{R}^{|E| \times p}$ are used to construct an average embedding of $Z_{t-1}$ as $Z_{t-1}^T E$. The final query is $g_t(q, z_{t-1}) \equiv \tilde{g}_t(q) + Z_{t-1}^T E$. Entity embeddings are computed as an average over word embeddings of the tokens in the entity's surface form. The computational cost of the question encoder $g_t(q)$ is $O(p^2)$. The total computational complexity to answer a query is $\tilde{O}(K \max\{K, \mu\} + Kp + p^2)$, with $O(\mu|E| + p|M|)$ memory for pre-computed matrices and the mention index.

PRETRAINING THE INDEX. End-to-end training of the mention encoder $f(m)$ with labeled QA data is challenging due to the need to recompute all mention embeddings after each parameter update. A staged training approach is adopted: first, pre-train $f(m)$, then compute and index all mention embeddings, keeping them fixed during downstream QA task training. Empirically, raw BERT representations do not capture the required information; thus, pretraining the encoder for better mention understanding is crucial. An alternative is to fine-tune BERT on SQuAD, but SQuAD's limited dataset and focus prevent it from effectively training for entity- and relation-centric questions. Instead, the mention encoder is trained using distant supervision from a knowledge base (KB). Given a KB of facts $(e_1, R, e_2)$, and a corpus of entity-linked text passages $\{d_k\}$, tuples $(d, (e_1, R, e_2))$ are identified where $d$ mentions both $e_1$ and $e_2$. This data is used to train for slot-filling queries in a reading comprehension setup. The query $q$ is constructed from the surface form of $e_1$ and a natural language description of $R$ (e.g., "Jerry Garcia, birth place, ?"), and the answer $e_2$ is extracted from passage $d$. Using string representations in $q$ ensures similarity to the downstream task. In pretraining, the scoring function is applied over all spans $m$ in the passage: $s(m, e_1, q) \propto \exp \{f(s) \cdot g(q, e_1)\}$.

Oracle queries improve recall for d1 by 6.68% and for d2 by 49.09% compared to R@10 for single-hop queries. This means the final QA model needs to consider fewer documents to find supporting facts.

The final QA component of GOLDEN Retriever is based on Yang et al. (2018), which is based on BiDAF++ (Clark and Gardner, 2017). Two major changes were made. First, instead of concatenating all context paragraphs into one long string (which is sensitive to order), paragraphs are processed separately with shared encoder RNN parameters. This produces order-insensitive representations. Span offset scores are predicted from each paragraph independently and then aggregated with a global softmax. Second, all attention mechanisms in the original model were replaced with self-attention layers over the concatenated question and context. Question and context tokens are differentiated by a 0/1 feature at the input layer. Figure 4 illustrates the QA model architecture.

Experiments were conducted in the fullwiki setting of HOTPOTQA. HOTPOTQA is a QA dataset from English Wikipedia with approximately 113k questions. Each question requires the introduction paragraphs of two Wikipedia articles to answer. The dataset includes gold paragraphs, supporting fact sentences, and diverse reasoning strategies (e.g., missing entities, intersection, comparison). In the few-document setting, QA models are given ten paragraphs. In the open-domain fullwiki setting, models receive only the question and all of Wikipedia. This results in a significant improvement. For the query "George W. Bush", the page for the former US president is ranked at the top after reranking.

Oracle Query Generation
Three heuristics are employed to find semantic overlap between retrieval context and desired documents: longest common subsequence (LCS), longest common substring (LCSubStr), and overlap merging. Overlap merging looks for contiguous spans in retrieval context with high token overlap rates with the desired document. The overlap rate is determined by the total number of overlapping tokens divided by the total number of tokens considered in the span.

In all heuristics, stop words are ignored, and text is lowercased. The span in the retrieval context containing all overlapping words is returned. For example, if retrieval context is "the GOLDEN Retriever model on HOTPOTQA" and desired document is "GOLDEN Retriever on the HOTPOTQA dataset", overlapping terms are "GOLDEN", "Retriever", and "HOTPOTQA". The resulting candidate query is "GOLDEN Retriever model on HOTPOTQA".

Candidate oracle queries are generated by applying heuristics between {cleaned question, cleaned question without punctuation} x {cleaned document title, cleaned paragraph}. Cleaning involves stop word removal and lowercasing. Generated oracle queries are launched against Elasticsearch to determine the rank of the desired paragraph. If multiple candidate queries place the desired paragraph in the top 5, candidate queries are further ranked by metrics like query length to determine the final oracle query for training query generators.

Training Details
Query Generators
Once oracle queries are generated, query generators are trained to emulate them. The best model is chosen based on F1 in span selection on the dev set. Hyperparameters for both query generators (G1 and G2) are reported.

Question Answering Model
The final question answering component is trained with paragraphs produced by oracle queries (5 from each hop, 10 in total). Documents d1 and d2 are inserted to replace the lowest ranking paragraph in each hop if not already present.

The model is based on Yang et al. (2018) and reuses default hyperparameters where possible. Differences include optimization with Adam (default hyperparameters) instead of stochastic gradient descent with a larger batch size of 64. The learning rate is annealed by 0.5 with a patience of 3. Gradients are clipped to a maximum l2 norm of 5. A 10% dropout is applied, and the hidden size is increased to 128. The supporting facts loss is multiplied by 10 before mixing with the span prediction loss. The model reads 10 context paragraphs, with each paragraph limited to at most 400 tokens including the title.

We propose leveraging text-based IR engines for interpretability and generating search queries at each reasoning step. In the first hop, GOLDEN Retriever receives the original question q and generates a query q1 to retrieve supporting document d1. For subsequent steps (k = 2, . . . , S), it generates a query qk from the question and available context (q, d1, . . . , dk-1), allowing query generation based on revealed information.

GOLDEN Retriever is more efficient, scalable, and interpretable than neural retrieval methods because it doesn't require a QA-specific IR engine tuned to a particular dataset, simplifying the addition of new documents or question types. Its natural language query generation is human-friendly. A key challenge is efficiently training query generation models due to the vast search space and non-differentiable IR engines.

**Query Generation**
For each reasoning step, a search query is generated given the original question q and retrieved documents. This is formulated as a QA task, mapping a question and context to a search query that retrieves the next supporting document.

To limit the query space, we use a QA model that extracts text spans from the context, rather than generating free-form text. We employ DrQA's Document Reader model, a lightweight recurrent neural network QA model successful in few-document QA.

For each reasoning step k (1 to S), given question q and retrieval context Ck (ideally containing gold supporting documents d1, . . . , dk-1), we generate a search query qk to retrieve dk:
qk = Gk(q, Ck)
where Gk is the query generator. This query is used to search for top n documents, which are concatenated with the context:
Ck+1 = Ck ><IRn(qk)
where IRn(qk) retrieves the top n documents using qk, and C1 = q. The final question q and context CS are then fed to a few-document QA component.

During training, if dk is not retrieved, the lowest-ranking document is replaced with dk before concatenation to ensure downstream models have necessary context.

Conclusion: GOLDEN (Gold Entity) Retriever is an open-domain multi-hop question answering system for scalable multi-hop reasoning. It improves gold supporting fact recall through iterative reasoning and retrieval, yielding competitive performance. Generating natural language queries per reasoning step makes GOLDEN Retriever more interpretable than previous neural retrieval approaches, facilitating model behavior understanding and verification.

**3 Model**
This section formally defines open-domain multi-hop question answering and motivates the architecture of the proposed GOLDEN (Gold Entity) Retriever model. It details query generation components, their supervision signals, and concludes with the QA component.

**3.1 Problem Statement**
Open-domain multi-hop QA involves a question `q` and `S` relevant supporting context documents `d1, ..., dS` containing the answer `a`. These documents form a reasoning chain from a large corpus `D` where `|D| >> S`. Document connections are usually via shared entities or textual similarities, without a predefined schema.

In contrast, the few-document setting presents a QA system with a small set of documents `D_few-doc = {d1, ..., dS, d'_1, ..., d'_D}`, where `d'_i` are distractor documents. This setting tests multi-hop reasoning with gold documents and a bounded computational budget, but is not realistic. An open-domain QA system must locate all gold supporting documents from `D` independently. For multi-hop questions, not all gold documents are easily retrievable from the original question alone.

To address gold context discoverability, a single-hop retrieve-and-read approach using the original question as a search query is insufficient. The GOLDEN Retriever addresses this by iterating between retrieving more documents and reading context over multiple rounds.

**3.2 Model Overview**
The challenge in open-domain multi-hop QA is that the user's information need (`q` -> `a`) cannot be satisfied by an information retrieval (IR) system solely based on the similarity between the question `q` and the documents. The true information need unfolds through progressive reasoning and discovery of supporting facts. Relying solely on a similarity-based IR system is problematic because the pool of relevant documents grows exponentially with reasoning hops.

The GOLDEN (Gold Entity) Retriever uses gold document information available at training time to iteratively query for more relevant supporting documents during each reasoning hop. Instead of using the original question to retrieve all supporting facts or building computationally expensive search engines, it leverages text-based IR engines for interpretability and generates different search queries as each reasoning step unfolds. In the first hop, the GOLDEN Retriever is presented with

*(Figure 2 shows an overview of GOLDEN Retriever: Given an open-domain multi-hop question, the model iteratively retrieves more context documents, concatenates them, and feeds them to a QA model for answering.)*

The central innovation is that at each step, the model uses IR results from previous hops of reasoning to generate a new natural language query and retrieve new evidence to answer the original question. For the example in Figure 1, GOLDEN would first generate a query to retrieve Armada (novel) based on the question, then query for Ernest Cline based on newly gained knowledge in that article. This allows GOLDEN to leverage off-the-shelf, general-purpose IR systems to scale open-domain multi-hop reasoning to millions of documents efficiently and in an interpretable manner. Combined with a QA module that extends BiDAF++ (Clark and Gardner, 2017), our final system outperforms the best previously published system on the open-domain (fullwiki) setting of HOTPOTQA without using powerful pretrained language models like BERT (Devlin et al., 2019).

The main contributions of this paper are: (a) a novel iterative retrieve-and-read framework capable of multi-hop reasoning in open-domain QA. (b) a natural language query generation approach that guarantees interpretability in the multi-hop evidence gathering process. (c) an efficient training procedure to enable query generation with minimal supervision signal that significantly boosts recall of gold supporting documents in retrieval.

Open-domain question answering (QA) inspired by the series of TREC QA competitions. Chen et al. (2017) were among the first to adapt neural QA models to the open-domain setting. They built a simple inverted index lookup with TF-IDF on the English Wikipedia, and used the question as the query to retrieve top 5 results for a reader model to produce answers with. Recent work on open-domain question answering largely follows this retrieve-and-read approach, and focuses on improving the information retrieval component with question answering performance in consideration (Nishida et al., 2018; Kratzwald and Feuerriegel, 2018; Nogueira et al., 2019). However, these one-step retrieve-and-read approaches are fundamentally ill-equipped to address questions that require multi-hop reasoning, especially when necessary evidence is not readily retrievable with the question.

Multi-hop QA datasets. QAngaroo (Welbl et al., 2018) and HOTPOTQA (Yang et al., 2018) are among the largest-scale multi-hop QA datasets to date. While the former is constructed around a knowledge base and the knowledge schema therein, the latter adopts a free-form question generation process in crowdsourcing and span-based evaluation. Both datasets feature a few-document setting where the gold supporting facts are provided along with a small set of distractors to ease the computational burden. However, researchers have shown that this sometimes results in gameable contexts, and thus does not always test the model's capability of multi-hop reasoning (Chen and Durrett, 2019; Min et al., 2019a). Therefore, in this work, we focus on the fullwiki setting of HOTPOTQA, which features a truly open-domain setting with more diverse questions.

Multi-hop QA systems. At a broader level, the need for multi-step searches, query task decomposition, and subtask extraction has been clearly recognized in the IR community (Hassan Awaladallah et al., 2014; Mehrotra et al., 2016; Mehrotra and Yilmaz, 2017), but multi-hop QA has only recently been studied closely with the release of large-scale datasets. Much research has focused on enabling multi-hop reasoning in question answering models in the few-document setting, e.g., by modeling entity graphs (De Cao et al., 2019) or scoring answer candidates against the context (Zhong et al., 2019). These approaches, however, suffer from scalability issues when the number of supporting documents and/or answer candidates grow beyond a few dozen. Ding et al. (2019) apply entity graph modeling to HOTPOTQA, where they expand a small entity graph starting from the question to arrive at the context for the QA model. However, centered around entity names, this model risks missing purely descriptive clues in the question. Das et al. (2019) propose a neural retriever trained with distant supervision to bias towards paragraphs containing answers to the given questions, which is then used in a multi-step reader-reasoner framework. This does not fundamentally address the discoverability issue in open-domain multi-hop QA, however, because usually not all the evidence can be directly retrieved with the question. Besides, the neural retrieval model lacks explainability, which is crucial in real-world applications. Talmor and Berant (2018), instead, propose to answer multi-hop questions at scale by decomposing the question into sub-questions and perform iterative retrieval and question answering, which shares very similar motivations as our work.

We always detokenize a generated search query before sending it to Elasticsearch, which has its own preprocessing pipeline. Since all questions in HOTPOTQA require exactly two supporting documents, we fix the number of retrieval steps of GOLDEN Retriever to S = 2. A stopping criterion is required to determine when to stop retrieving for more supporting documents and perform few-document question answering. During training and evaluation, we set the number of retrieved documents added to the retrieval context to 5 for each retrieval step, so that the total number of paragraphs our final QA model considers is 10, for a fair comparison. We include hyperparameters and training details in Appendix C for reproducibility.

We compare the end-to-end performance of GOLDEN Retriever against several QA systems on the HOTPOTQA dataset: (1) a baseline system, (2) CogQA, the top-performing previously published system, and (3) other high-ranking systems on the leaderboard. GOLDEN Retriever is much better at locating the correct supporting facts from Wikipedia compared to CogQA and most other top-ranking systems. However, the QA performance is handicapped because we do not make use of pretrained contextualization models (e.g., BERT) that these systems use. We expect a boost in QA performance from adopting these more powerful question answering models, especially ones that are tailored to perform few-document multi-hop reasoning.

To understand the contribution of GOLDEN Retriever's iterative retrieval process compared to that of the IR engine, we compare its performance against two baseline systems on the dev set: one that retrieves 10 supporting paragraphs from Elasticsearch with the original question, and one that uses the IR engine presented in HOTPOTQA. In all cases, we use the QA component in GOLDEN Retriever for the final question answering step. Replacing the hand-engineered IR engine with Elasticsearch results in some gain in recall of the gold documents, but that does not translate to a significant improvement in QA performance. Elasticsearch is only able to retrieve both gold documents for 36.91% of the dev set questions, in comparison to 28.21% from the IR engine in HOTPOTQA. In contrast, GOLDEN Retriever improves this percentage to 61.01%, almost doubling the recall over the single-hop baseline, providing the QA component a much better set of context documents to predict answers from.

For multi-hop questions, traditional retrieval-extraction frameworks can limit follow-up models. Paragraphs distant from the question may share few common words or semantic relations, leading to retrieval failure. These paragraphs can be found by iteratively expanding with clues in our framework.

Algorithm 1 outlines the CogQA framework. After initialization, an iterative process for graph expansion and reasoning begins. In each step, a frontier node x is visited. System 1 reads para[x] using clues and the question Q, extracting spans and generating semantic vector sem[x, Q, clues]. Concurrently, System 2 updates hidden representation X and prepares clues[y, G] for successor node y. The final prediction is based on X.

Implementation

The CogQA framework implementation involves defining the concrete models for System 1 and 2, and the form of clues.

Our implementation uses BERT as System 1 and GNN as System 2. Clues[x, G] are sentences from predecessor nodes' paragraphs from which x was extracted. Raw sentences are passed as clues, not computed hidden states, for easier System 1 training. Raw sentences are self-contained and independent of previous iterative step computations, decoupling training at different steps for efficiency gains. Details are in SS 3.4. Hidden representations X for graph nodes are updated via GNN propagation.

The retrieval community dates back to the 1990s. DrQA, a neural model, extracts accurate answers from retrieved paragraphs, advancing the retrieval-extraction framework. Improvements enhance retrieval through heuristic sampling or reinforcement learning, but complex reasoning requires framework revisits.

CogQA, a new framework, tackles multi-hop machine reading at scale. Its cognitive graph organizes reasoning, offering entity-level explainability. Implementation with BERT and GNN achieves state-of-the-art results on the HotpotQA dataset.

Future research directions include leveraging neural logic techniques in CogQA's System 2 for improved reliability, benefiting from the cognitive graph's explicit structure. Prospective architectures combining attention and recurrent mechanisms may enhance System 1's capacity by optimizing system interaction. The framework could generalize to other cognitive tasks like conversational AI and sequential recommendation.

Cognitive Graph QA (CogQA) addresses challenges in multi-hop reading comprehension QA. Inspired by dual process theory, CogQA employs functionally distinct System 1 and System 2 modules. System 1 extracts question-relevant entities and answer candidates from paragraphs, encoding their semantic information. Extracted entities are organized into a cognitive graph, simulating working memory. System 2 reasons over this graph, guiding System 1 to extract subsequent entities. This iterative process continues until all possible answers are identified, with the final answer selected based on System 2's reasoning. An efficient implementation using BERT and Graph Neural Network (GNN) is presented.

Contributions:
*   Novel CogQA framework for multi-hop reading comprehension QA at scale, aligning with human cognition.
*   Cognitive graph structure provides ordered, entity-level explainability and supports relational reasoning.
*   BERT and GNN-based implementation significantly outperforms previous works and competitors across all metrics.

The reasoning ability of humans relies on relational information structures. A directed graph structure is adopted for step-by-step deduction and exploration in the cognitive process of multi-hop QA. In this reading comprehension setting, each node in the cognitive graph G represents an entity or a potential answer, interchangeably denoted as node x. System 1 reads the introductory paragraph (para[x]) for entity x and extracts answer candidates and useful next-hop entities. The graph G is expanded with these new nodes, providing structure for System 2. System 2 performs deep learning-based reasoning by computing hidden representations X of nodes. System 1 summarizes para[x] into a semantic vector as the initial hidden representation for span extraction. System 2 then updates X based on the graph structure for downstream prediction.

Explainability is achieved through explicit reasoning paths in the cognitive graph, which can display joint or loopy reasoning processes. Clues, a flexible concept, refer to information from predecessors that guide System 1 in extracting spans. Nodes with new incoming edges also require revisits due to new clues; both newly added nodes and those with new incoming edges are referred to as frontier nodes. Scalability is ensured as the framework accesses specific paragraphs by their title indexes, preventing significant growth in time consumption with more paragraphs.

We propose a new CogQA framework for multi-hop question answering in web-scale documents. The framework gradually builds a cognitive graph in an iterative process by coordinating an implicit extraction module (System 1) and an explicit reasoning module (System 2). Our framework provides explainable reasoning paths. Our implementation based on BERT and graph neural network (GNN) efficiently handles millions of documents for multi-hop reasoning questions in the HotpotQA fullwiki dataset, achieving a winning joint F1 score of 34.9 on the leaderboard.

Deep learning models have made significant strides in machine reading comprehension, outperforming humans on single paragraph question answering (QA) benchmarks. However, three main challenges remain: 1) Reasoning ability. Multi-hop QA requires complex reasoning beyond single-paragraph QA models. 2) Explainability. Explicit reasoning paths are vital for the reliability of QA systems, requiring ordered and entity-level explainability. 3) Scalability. Existing QA systems typically use a retrieval-extraction framework, which is a compromise between single-paragraph QA and scalable information retrieval.

Insights from human cognitive processes can address these challenges. Dual process theory suggests that our brains first retrieve relevant information via an implicit, unconscious process (System 1), followed by an explicit, conscious reasoning process (System 2). System 1 extracts information, while System 2 performs sequential thinking for deeper relational understanding. For complex reasoning, these systems coordinate iterative fast and slow thinking.

Results
Primary Results
Tables show main results on the HotpotQA and SQuAD-Open datasets. In the HotpotQA distractor setting, the paragraph reader improves the baseline reader results, increasing joint EM and F1 scores by 17.12 (148%) and 13.22 (32%) points, respectively. In the full wiki setting, three methods of retrieval are compared: TF-IDF (using only the TF-IDF heuristic, feeding all possible paragraph pairs from the top-10 paragraphs to the reader), Sentence-level (using MUPPET with sentence-level encodings), and Paragraph-level (using MUPPET with paragraph-level encodings, without sentence information). Both MUPPET methods significantly outperform the naive TF-IDF retriever. The models are ranked second in the HotpotQA full wiki setting (test set) leaderboard as of March 5, 2019. For SQuAD-Open, the sentence-level method established state-of-the-art results, improving the current non-BERT (Devlin et al., 2018) state-of-the-art by 4.6 (13%) and 3.6 (8%) EM and F1 points, respectively. This demonstrates the encoder's utility for both multi-hop and single-hop questions.

Retrieval Recall Analysis
The performance of the TF-IDF retriever for HotpotQA is analyzed. The retriever successfully retrieves at least one gold paragraph for each question (above 90% with the top-32 paragraphs) but fails to retrieve both gold paragraphs. This highlights the need for an efficient multi-hop retrieval approach to complement or replace classic information retrieval methods.

Effect of Narrowing the Search Space
Performance of the method is shown as a function of the search space size in the last retrieval iteration. For SQuAD-Open, the TF-IDF retriever initially retrieves documents, which are split into paragraphs to form the search space. A search space of top-k paragraphs limits potential recall to that of the top-k paragraphs retrieved by the TF-IDF retriever. This is suboptimal for very small k, as the TF-IDF retriever's performance is insufficient. The models do not benefit from indefinitely increasing the search space, suggesting they are not as robust to noise as desired.

Effectiveness of Sentence-Level Encodings: Our method uses sentence-level encodings for paragraph retrieval. This approach's significance is tested in Figures 5b and 5c. Sentence-level encodings improve state-of-the-art results on SQuAD-Open but not on HotpotQA. This difference is hypothesized to be due to dataset creation methods. In SQuAD, each paragraph serves as context for multiple questions, meaning facts essential to a paragraph's gist might not be encapsulated in its representation. In contrast, most HotpotQA training set paragraphs serve as context for at most one question.

Related Work: Chen et al. (2017) introduced neural methods for open-domain QA with textual knowledge sources, proposing DrQA, a pipeline with a TF-IDF retriever and a neural network for answer span detection. To enhance TF-IDF retrieval, many works use Distant Supervision (DS) for re-ranking paragraphs. Wang et al. (2018a) used reinforcement learning for end-to-end training of a re-ranker and RC component, showing advantages over DS alone. Min et al. (2018) trained a sentence selector, demonstrating the effectiveness of reading minimal contexts. Lin et al. (2018) proposed a denoising method to address potential mislabeling from DS. These re-ranking methods are limited by the number of paragraphs they can process due to joint question-paragraph reading. Our approach precomputes paragraph representations for efficient large-scale retrieval. Lee et al. (2018) learned encoding functions for questions and paragraphs, ranking paragraphs by dot-product similarity, with improvements from answer aggregation methods. Seo et al. (2018) proposed phrase-indexed QA (PI-QA), which encodes answers and questions independently, retrieving answers via MIPS, presenting a more challenging task. Das et al. (2019) introduced a framework with multi-step interaction between a retriever and reader to refine question representation for more accurate retrieval, complementary to our method for single-hop questions and not handling multi-hop domains. Memory Networks (Weston et al., 2015) are another related line of work, consisting of cells storing vectors and modules for memory manipulation, with variations like end-to-end Memory Networks, Key-Value Memory Networks, and Hierarchical Memory Networks.

Concluding Remarks: We present MUPPET, a novel method for multi-hop paragraph retrieval, demonstrating its efficacy in single- and multi-hop QA datasets. A challenge in open-domain multi-hop QA is the lack of supervision, partially addressed in single-hop QA by distant supervision. Future work aims to tackle this to enable learning beyond two retrieval iterations. An improvement could involve allowing the retriever to automatically determine the need for further retrieval.

For multi-hop retrieval, given a question Q, its encoding q is obtained. This is transformed into a search vector qs for retrieving top-k relevant paragraphs {P Q 1, P Q 2, . . . , P Q k} from KS using MIPS. In each subsequent iteration, retrieved paragraphs reformulate the search vector, producing k new vectors {~qs 1, ~qs 2, . . . , ~qs k}. ## Paragraph and Question Encoder

The encoder model, f, takes a paragraph P with k sentences (s1, s2, . . . , sk) and m tokens (t1, t2, . . . , tm), where si = (ti1, ti2, . . . , til) and l is sentence length. The encoder generates k d-dimensional encodings (s1, s2, . . . , sk) = f(P), one for each sentence. This differs from prior work using single fixed-size representations.

### Word Embedding

Each token t is embedded into a vector t using character-level and word-level information. The word-level embedding tw uses pretrained word embeddings. The character-level embedding tc for a token with lt characters (tc1, tc2, . . . , tclt) is obtained by embedding each character tc i into a fixed-size vector. These character embeddings are passed through a 1D convolutional neural network, followed by max-pooling over the filter dimension, producing a fixed-size character-level representation tc = max CNN(tc1, tc2, . . . , tclt). The final word representation is the concatenation of word-level and character-level embeddings: t = [tw; tc].

### Recurrent Layer

A bidirectional GRU processes word representations to obtain contextualized word representations: (c1, c2, . . . , cm) = BiGRU(t1, t2, . . . , tm).

### Sentence-wise Max-pooling

Contextualized representations are chunked into sentence groups. Max-pooling is applied over the time dimension of each sentence group to obtain d-dimensional sentence representations: si = max(ci1, ci2, . . . , cil).

The encoding q of a question Q is computed similarly: q = f(Q). A single vector is produced for each question by applying max-pooling over all question words, disregarding sentence information.

## Reformulation Component

The reformulation component takes a paragraph P and a question Q, producing a single vector ~q. Contextualized word representations (cq 1, cq 2, . . . , cqnq) for Q and (cp 1, cp 2, . . . , cpn p) for P are obtained using the same embedding and recurrent layers. These are passed through a bidirectional attention layer. Attention between question word i and paragraph word j is computed as: aij = wa1 * cqi + wa2 * cpj + wa3 * (cqi cpj).

Paragraph Reader
The paragraph reader receives a question Q and a paragraph P as input and extracts the most probable answer span to Q from P. We use the shared-norm model presented by Clark and Gardner (2018), referred to as S-norm. The model's architecture is similar to the encoder's. First, Q and P are processed separately to obtain their contextualized token representations. These are then passed through a bidirectional attention layer, similar to the encoder's reformulation layer, with the roles of the question and paragraph switched. The bidirectional attention representations are further passed through a residual connection, using a self-attention layer between the bidirectional GRU and a linear layer. The self-attention mechanism is similar to the bidirectional attention layer, but operates between the paragraph and itself. Question-to-paragraph attention is not used, and $a_{ij} = -\infty$ if $i = j$. The summed outputs of the residual connection are passed to the prediction layer. The inputs to the prediction layer are passed through a bidirectional GRU followed by a linear layer that predicts the answer span start scores. The hidden layers of that GRU are concatenated with the input and passed through another bidirectional GRU and linear layer to predict the answer span end scores.

Training
An input sample for the paragraph reader consists of a question and a single context (Q, P). We optimize the same negative log-likelihood function used in the S-norm model for the span start boundaries:
$L_{start} = -\log \frac{P_{Q \in PQ} P_{j \in P} \sum_{k \in A_j} e^{s_{kj}}}{\sum_{j \in P} \sum_{i=1}^{n_j} e^{s_{ij}}}$,
where $PQ$ is the set of paragraphs paired with the same question Q, $A_j$ is the set of tokens that start an answer span in the j-th paragraph, and $s_{ij}$ is the score given to the i-th token in the j-th paragraph. The same formulation is used for the span end boundaries, so that the final objective function is the sum of the two: $L_{span} = L_{start} + L_{end}$.

Paragraph Reader Extension for HotpotQA
HotpotQA requires predicting an answer span, yes/no answers, and supporting facts for explainability. We extend the paragraph reader to support these predictions.

Yes/No Prediction
We propose that the question alone can determine if the answer is span-based or yes/no-based. A fixed-size vector representing the question is created using max-pooling over the first bidirectional GRU's states. This representation is passed through a linear layer to predict whether the question is yes/no-based or span-based. If span-based, the answer span is predicted from the context using the original span prediction layer. If yes/no-based, question-aware context representations are encoded into a fixed-size vector by max-pooling over the outputs of the residual self-attention layer. This vector is then passed through a linear layer to predict a yes/no answer.

**SQuAD-Open**
Training data is gathered as follows: For each question in the original SQuAD dataset, the original context paragraph is the single relevant (positive) paragraph. Approximately 12 irrelevant (negative) paragraphs are gathered for each question:

**HotpotQA**
Paragraphs for training the encoder are the gold and distractor paragraphs from the original HotpotQA training set. Each training sample consists of a question and two paragraphs, (Q, P1, P2), where P1 is from the first iteration retrieval and P2 is from the second. Sample types for each question are created:
1.  **Gold:** Both paragraphs are gold paragraphs. P1 and P2 are positive.
2.  **First gold, second distractor:** P1 is a gold paragraph (positive). P2 can be a random paragraph, P1, or a distractor with probabilities 0.05, 0.1, and 0.85, respectively. P2 is negative.
3.  **First distractor, second gold:** P1 is a distractor or a random paragraph (probabilities 0.9 and 0.1, respectively). P2 is a gold paragraph. P1 and P2 are negative.
4.  **All distractors:** Both P1 and P2 are sampled from the question's distractors. Both are negative.
5.  **Gold from another question:** A gold paragraph pair from a different question. Both paragraphs are negative.

Sample type 1 is mandatory as it contains purely positive examples. Type 2 helps learn valuable reformulation without relying solely on the first paragraph. Type 3 complements type 2, teaching irrelevance if the first paragraph is irrelevant. Type 3 is used for random negative sampling. Type 4 ensures relevancy is not determined solely by the paragraph pair but also by the question.

Each training batch includes three samples for each question: one gold sample (type 1) and two from the other four types with probabilities 0.35, 0.35, 0.25, and 0.05, respectively.

A batch size of 75 (25 unique questions) is used. The margin is set to g = 1 in Equation (1) and l = 1 in Equation (2) for both prediction iterations. Paragraph length is limited to 600 tokens.

This paper addresses multi-hop open-domain Question Answering (QA). This task challenges due to the need for simultaneous textual reasoning and efficient searching. We introduce a method to retrieve multiple supporting paragraphs from a large knowledge base that contain necessary evidence to answer a question. Our method iteratively retrieves supporting paragraphs by creating a joint vector representation of the question and each paragraph. Retrieval considers contextualized sentence-level representations of paragraphs within the knowledge source. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on SQuAD-Open (single-hop) and HotpotQA (multi-hop) datasets.

Textual Question Answering (QA) involves answering natural language questions using provided contexts. This field, within natural language understanding, has seen significant interest due to promising deep learning results, facilitated by large-scale QA datasets like TriviaQA and SQuAD. Current state-of-the-art methods even surpass human performance on certain tasks.

Reading Comprehension (RC) is a common QA task where each question is paired with a small number of paragraphs from which an answer can be inferred. The goal is to extract the correct answer or determine if the question is unanswerable. Most large-scale RC datasets focus on single-hop reasoning, where the answer can be inferred from one paragraph. Multi-hop reasoning requires combining evidence from multiple sources. An example question requiring multi-hop reasoning necessitates inferring the manager's identity from one context before inferring the answer from another.

Open-domain QA involves answering questions without accompanying contexts. This requires locating relevant contexts from a large knowledge source (e.g., Wikipedia) and then using an RC component to extract the answer. Previous methods used a TF-IDF based retriever for documents, followed by a neural RC component. While this approach works for single-hop reasoning, its performance degrades significantly for open-domain multi-hop reasoning.

We propose iterative multi-hop retrieval for this task, which involves iteratively retrieving necessary evidence.

Multi-paragraph reasoning is indispensable for open-domain question answering (OpenQA). This work proposes a knowledge-enhanced graph neural network (KGNN) for reasoning over multiple paragraphs with entities. KGNN utilizes relational facts from a knowledge graph to build an entity graph and explicitly capture entity relatedness. Experiments show KGNN outperforms baselines on the HotpotQA dataset in both distractor and full wiki settings. Further analysis indicates KGNN is effective and robust with more retrieved paragraphs.

Open-domain question answering (OpenQA) aims to answer questions based on large-scale knowledge sources, such as an unlabelled corpus. Recent years have seen increased interest in OpenQA, with the availability of large-scale datasets like Quasar, SearchQA, and TriviaQA. Numerous OpenQA models have been proposed, achieving promising results on various benchmarks.

However, most questions in previous OpenQA datasets require reasoning within a single paragraph or a single-hop across paragraphs. The HotpotQA dataset was developed to facilitate the advancement of OpenQA systems in handling multi-paragraph reasoning. Multi-paragraph reasoning is an important and practical problem for more intelligent OpenQA. Existing OpenQA systems generally handle multiple paragraphs in two ways: (1) treating each paragraph individually, hindering inter-paragraph reasoning; or (2) concatenating all paragraphs into a single long text, which is time and memory intensive.

To achieve a multi-paragraph reasoning system, a knowledge-enhanced graph neural network (KGNN) is proposed. KGNN first builds an entity graph from all named entities in the paragraphs, adding co-reference edges if an entity appears in different paragraphs. To explicitly capture entity relatedness, relational facts from a knowledge graph (KG) are used to build a relational entity graph, adding relation edges if two entities have a relation in the KG. Reasoning information is believed to be captured through propagation over this relational entity graph. For instance, to reason about an entity like "Wildest Dreams," KGNN requires two types of one-hop reasoning: one based on the entity appearing in multiple paragraphs and another based on the relational fact (Wildest Dreams, lyrics by, Max Martin and Shellback).

The primary contribution is a novel reasoning module combined with knowledge. Experiments demonstrate that reasoning over entities significantly improves the model's performance compared to baselines on the HotpotQA dataset. Analysis shows KGNN is robust and capable of handling extensive texts.

2 Task Definition
Explainable multi-hop QA is re-defined to include the RC and RTE tasks.

Definition 1. Explainable Multi-hop QA
Input: Context C (multiple texts), Query Q (text)
Output: Answer Type AT (label), Answer String AS (text), Evidence E (multiple texts)

The Context C is treated as one connected text in the model. If the connected C is over 2000 words, it is truncated. The Query Q is the query. The model answers Q with an answer type AT or an answer string AS. The Answer Type AT is selected from answer candidates, such as 'Yes'. The answer candidates depend on the task setting. The Answer String AS exists only if there are not enough answer candidates to answer Q. The answer string AS is a short span in C. Evidence E consists of sentences in C and is required to answer Q.

For RC, HotpotQA is used. In HotpotQA, answer candidates are 'Yes', 'No', and 'Span'. The answer string AS exists if and only if the answer type AT is 'Span'. C consists of ten Wikipedia paragraphs. Evidence E consists of two or more sentences in C.

For RTE, FEVER is used. In FEVER, answer candidates are 'Supports', 'Refutes', and 'Not Enough Info'. The answer string AS does not exist. C is the Wikipedia database. Evidence E consists of sentences in C.

3 Proposed Method
This section explains the overall model architecture, which contains our model as a module, and then the details of our QFE.

3.1 Model Architecture
Except for the evidence layer, our model is the same as the baseline (Clark and Gardner, 2018) used in HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018). Figure 2 shows the model architecture. The input of the model is the context C and the query Q.

The Word Embedding Layer encodes C and Q as sequences of word vectors. A word vector is the concatenation of a pre-trained word embedding and a character-based embedding obtained using a CNN (Kim, 2014). The outputs are C1  Rlwxdw, Q1 Rmwxdw, where lw is the length (in words) of C, mw is the length of Q and dw is the size of the word vector.

The Context Layer encodes C1, Q1 as contextual vectors C2 Rlwx2dc, Q2 Rmwx2dc by using a bi-directional RNN (Bi-RNN), where dc is the output size of a uni-directional RNN.

The Matching Layer encodes C2, Q2 as matching vectors C3 Rlwxdc by using bi-directional attention (Seo et al., 2017), a Bi-RNN, and self-attention (Wang et al., 2017).

The Evidence Layer first encodes C3 as [--C4; --C4] Rlwx2dc by a Bi-RNN. Let j1(i) be the index of the first word of the i-th sentence in C and j2(i) be the index of the last word. The vector of the i-th sentence is defined as:
xi = [----c4,j2(i); ----c4,j1(i)] R2dc.
Here, X Rlsx2dc is the sentence-level context vectors, where ls is the number of sentences of C. QFE, described later, receives sentence-level context vectors X Rlsx2dc and the contextual query vectors Q2 Rmwx2dc as Y. QFE outputs the probability distribution that the i-th sentence is the evidence:
Pr(i) = QFE(X, Y = Q2). (1)
Then, the evidence layer concatenates the word-level vectors and the sentence-level vectors:
c5,j = [c3,j; xi(j)] R3dc,
where the j-th word in C is included in the i(j)-th sentence in C.

The Answer Layer predicts the answer type AT and the answer string AS from C5. The layer has stacked Bi-RNNs. The output of each Bi-RNN is mapped to the probability distribution by the fully connected layer and the softmax function.
For RC, the layer has three stacked Bi-RNNs. Each probability indicates the start of the answer string, ^AS1 Rlw, the end of the answer string ^AS2 Rlw, and the answer type, ^AT R3. For RTE, the layer has one Bi-RNN. The probability indicates the answer type.

Loss Function:
The model uses multi-task learning with a loss function L = LA+LE, where LA is the loss of the answer and LE is the loss of the evidence. The answer loss LA is the sum of the cross-entropy losses for all probability distributions obtained by the answer layer. The evidence loss LE is defined in subsection 3.3.

3.2 Query Focused Extractor
Query Focused Extractor (QFE) is shown as the red box in Figure 2. QFE is an extension of the extractive summarization model of Chen and Bansal.

Summarization utilizes an encoder-decoder architecture. Sentence-level extractive summarization selects content for abstractive summarization by extracting sentences in order of importance and editing them. This model has been extended for evidence extraction, prioritizing importance over the original order used by conventional models.

Answering while Summarizing: Multi-task Learning for Multi-hop QA with Evidence Extraction

Question answering (QA) using textual sources for purposes such as reading comprehension (RC) has attracted much attention. This study focuses on the task of explainable multi-hop QA, which requires the system to return the answer with evidence sentences by reasoning and gathering disjoint pieces of the reference texts. It proposes the Query Focused Extractor (QFE) model for evidence extraction and uses multi-task learning with the QA model. QFE is inspired by extractive summarization models; compared with the existing method, which extracts each evidence sentence independently, it sequentially extracts evidence sentences by using an RNN with an attention mechanism on the question sentence. It enables QFE to consider the dependency among the evidence sentences and cover important information in the question sentence. Experimental results show that QFE with a simple RC baseline model achieves a state-of-the-art evidence extraction score on HotpotQA. Although designed for RC, it also achieves a state-of-the-art evidence extraction score on FEVER, which is a recognizing textual entailment task on a large textual database.

Reading comprehension (RC) is a task that uses textual sources to answer any question. It has seen significant progress since the publication of numerous datasets such as SQuAD. To achieve the goal of RC, systems must be able to reason over disjoint pieces of information in the reference texts. Recently, multi-hop question answering (QA) datasets focusing on this capability, such as QAngaroo and HotpotQA, have been released.

Multi-hop QA faces two challenges. The first is the difficulty of reasoning. It is difficult for the system to find the disjoint pieces of information as evidence and reason using the multiple pieces of such evidence. The second challenge is interpretability. The evidence used to reason is not necessarily located close to the answer, so it is difficult for users to verify the answer.

HotpotQA, an explainable multi-hop QA dataset, provides the evidence sentences of the answer for supervised learning. The evidence extraction in multi-hop QA is more difficult than that in other QA problems because the question itself may not provide a clue for finding evidence sentences. In this task, the system finds an evidence sentence by relying on another evidence sentence. The capability of being able to explicitly extract evidence is an advance towards meeting these challenges.

Here, we propose a Query Focused Extractor (QFE) that is based on a summarization model. We regard the evidence extraction of the explainable multi-hop QA as a query-focused summarization task. Query-focused summarization is the task of summarizing the source document with regard to the given query. QFE sequentially extracts the evidence sentences by using an RNN with an attention mechanism on the question sentence, while the existing method extracts each evidence sentence independently. This query-aware recurrent structure enables QFE to consider the dependency among the evidence sentences and cover the important information in the question sentence.

Our overall model uses multi-task learning with a QA model for answer selection and QFE for evidence extraction. The multi-task learning with QFE is general in the sense that it can be combined with any QA model.

Moreover, we find that the recognizing textual entailment (RTE) task on a large textual database, FEVER, can be regarded as an explainable multi-hop QA task. We confirm that QFE effectively extracts the evidence both on HotpotQA for RC and on FEVER for RTE.

Our main contributions are as follows:
* We propose QFE for explainable multi-hop QA. We use the multi-task learning of the QA model for answer selection and QFE for evidence extraction.
* QFE adaptively determines the number of evidence sentences by considering the dependency among the evidence sentences and the coverage of the question.
* QFE achieves state-of-the-art performance on both HotpotQA and FEVER in terms of the evidence extraction score and comparable performance to competitive models in terms of the answer selection score. QFE is the first

Related Work

Reading Comprehension
RC is performed by matching the context and the query. Many RC datasets referring to multiple texts have been published, such as MS MARCO and TriviaQA. For these datasets, a document retrieval model is combined with a context-query matching model.
Techniques have been proposed for understanding multiple texts, such as connecting texts, and a combination of coarse reading and fine reading. However, most questions in RC require reasoning from just one sentence including the answer, with proportions over 63.2% in TriviaQA and 86.2% in MS MARCO.
This observation motivates multi-hop QA. HotpotQA is a task including supervised evidence extraction. QAngaroo is a task created using Wikipedia entity links. QAngaroo differs from our focus in two ways: (1) it lacks supervised evidence, and (2) its questions are inherently limited because the dataset is constructed using a knowledge base. MultiRC is an explainable multi-hop QA dataset that provides gold evidence sentences. However, comparing evidence extraction performance is difficult as its evaluation script and leaderboard do not report the evidence extraction score.
Since annotating evidence sentences is costly, unsupervised learning of evidence extraction is another important issue. Unsupervised learning for explainable multi-hop QA has been addressed, but the model is restricted to the multiple-choice setting.

Recognizing Textual Entailment
RTE is performed by sentence matching.
FEVER aims at verification and fact checking for RTE on a large database. FEVER requires three sub-tasks: document retrieval, evidence extraction, and answer prediction.
Previous work used pipelined models for these sub-tasks. In contrast, our approach performs evidence extraction and answer prediction simultaneously by regarding FEVER as an explainable multi-hop QA task.

V. CONCLUSION
UniDepthV2, a universal monocular metric depth estimation model, enhances generalization across diverse domains without requiring camera parameters at test time. Improvements in model architecture and new loss functions in the training objective allow UniDepthV2 to achieve state-of-the-art performance with improved computational efficiency, as verified by extensive zero-shot and fine-tuning evaluations. The training strategy also enables a flexible trade-off between inference speed and detail preservation by allowing variable input resolutions at test time while maintaining global scale consistency.

Camera conditioning and its role are analyzed, reporting results for the original UniDepth under the same training and evaluation setup. Evaluation uses four metrics: d1 (metric depth accuracy), SIlog (scale-invariant scene geometry), FA (3D estimation capability), and rA (monocular camera parameter estimation). All metrics are aggregated zero-shot performance across datasets.

Architecture modifications transform UniDepth [17] to UniDepthV2. Spherical harmonics (SH)-based encoding is removed due to inefficiency, reverting to standard Sine encoding. This change has minimal performance difference, hypothesized to be due to larger, diverse training data from different cameras reducing the encoding's impact. The attention mechanism is eliminated due to high computational cost, causing a significant performance drop (e.g., -4.3% for d1) but yielding over 2x efficiency improvement. The pure MLP-based decoder is replaced with ResNet blocks, introducing spatial 3 x 3 convolutions. This enhances performance by leveraging local spatial structure with minimal efficiency impact. Multi-resolution feature fusion from encoder to decoder, using an FPN-style design, is integrated. The final architecture significantly reduces computational cost while preserving performance, achieving similar results to the original UniDepth with one-third the computation.

LEG-SSI Loss: The effectiveness of the proposed LEG-SSI loss is evaluated. Its introduction leads to a 4.7% improvement in d1 and a 1.8% improvement in FA, contributing to metric accuracy and 3D estimation. rA also shows improvement, suggesting the loss leads to a less noisy training process and better encoder representations. Qualitative comparisons highlight the visual impact of the loss, particularly in refining depth discontinuities and reconstructing finer details.

Lcon Output Space: UniDepthV2 uses multiple instances of camera-conditioned depth features D|E across different decoder resolutions, unlike the original UniDepth's single conditioning point. This architectural shift suggests deep conditioning may not be optimal, as features at different resolutions encode varying abstraction levels. An investigation into applying the consistency loss (Lcon) from [17] shows minimal differences between applying it directly in the output space (Z) or within camera-conditioned features at each scale (D|E).

UniDepthV2 is implemented in PyTorch and CUDA. AdamW optimizer (b1 = 0.9, b2 = 0.999) is used with an initial learning rate of 5 x 10-5. Backbone weights learning rate is divided by 10 for every experiment. Weight decay is set to 0.1. Cosine Annealing is used as the learning rate and weight decay scheduler, starting from 30% of the training iterations. 300k optimization iterations are performed with a batch size of 128. Training time is 6 days on 16 NVIDIA 4090 with half precision. Dataset sampling uses a weighted sampler, with dataset weight equal to its number of scenes. Augmentations include geometric (random resizing, cropping, translation) and photometric (brightness, gamma, saturation, hue shift). Image ratio per batch is sampled between 2:1 and 1:2. ViT backbone is initialized with DINO-pre-trained weights. For ablations, 100k training steps are run with a ViT-S backbone.

Evaluation is performed on eight zero-shot validation sets, covering indoor and outdoor scenes. UniDepthV2 outperforms or matches all baselines. It excels in 3D estimation, with FA metric improvement ranging from 0.5% to 18.1% over the second-best method. It also outperforms UniDepth in most cases, except for the rA metric on IBims-1, DDAD, and NuScenes. Marginal improvements in camera parameter estimation (rA) suggest that limited diversity of training cameras is a challenge. Fine-tuning is performed on KITTI and NYU-Depth V2.

Despite achievements on established benchmarks, MMDE models face challenges in zero-shot scenarios, requiring robust generalization against appearance and geometry domain shifts.

General Monocular Metric Depth Estimation. Recent efforts focus on developing MMDE models for general depth prediction across diverse domains. These models leverage camera awareness by incorporating external camera parameters into computations or by normalizing shape or output depth based on intrinsic properties. A new paradigm aims to directly estimate the 3D scene from the input image without additional information beyond the RGB input. This approach, termed universal MMDE, requires no additional prior information at test time, such as camera information.

UniDepthV2. Most SotA MMDE methods assume access to camera intrinsics, blurring the line between pure depth estimation and actual 3D estimation. UniDepthV2 aims to create a universal MMDE model deployable in diverse scenarios without relying on external information like camera intrinsics, leading to 3D-space estimation by design. However, directly predicting 3D points from a single image without a proper internal representation neglects geometric prior knowledge, burdening the learning process with re-learning laws of perspective projection from data.

A pseudo-spherical representation of the output space disentangles camera rays' angles from depth. Preliminary studies indicate depth prediction benefits from prior information on the acquisition sensor, leading to a self-prompting camera operation. Further disentanglement is achieved through a geometric invariance loss, ensuring depth predictions remain invariant when conditioned on bootstrapped camera predictions, promoting robust camera-aware depth predictions. Additionally, spatial resolution is enhanced via an edge-guided normalized loss on depth prediction, forcing the network to learn sharp transitions in depth values and flat surfaces. The overall architecture and optimization are detailed.

3D Representation. The general-purpose nature of this MMDE method requires inferring both depth and camera intrinsics to make 3D predictions based only on imagery observations. The 3D output space is designed with a natural disentanglement of depth estimation and camera calibration sub-tasks. A pseudo-spherical representation is exploited, with the basis defined by azimuth, elevation, and log-depth (th,ph,zlog), contrasting with the Cartesian representation (x,y,z). This representation decouples camera (th,ph) and depth (zlog) components, ensuring their orthogonality by design, unlike the entanglement in Cartesian representation.

In this output space, the non-parametric dense representation of the camera is mathematically represented as a tensor C RHxW x2, where H and W are the height and width of the input image, and the last dimension corresponds to azimuth and elevation values. While backprojection in typical Cartesian space involves multiplying homogeneous camera rays and depth, backprojection in the proposed representation space accounts for the concatenation of camera and depth representations. Pencil of rays are defined as (r1, r2, r3) = K-1[u, v, 1]T, where K is the calibration matrix, u and v are pixel positions, and 1 is a vector of ones. Homogeneous camera rays (rx, ry) correspond to (r1/r3, r2/r3). This dense camera representation can be embedded via Sine encoding, with 64 harmonics per homogeneous ray dimension, resulting in 128 channels.

Self-Promptable Camera. The camera module is crucial for final 3D predictions as its angular dense output accounts for two dimensions of the output space: azimuth and elevation. These embeddings prompt the depth module to ensure bootstrapped prior knowledge of the input scene's global depth scale. This prompting avoids mode collapse in scene scale and alleviates the depth module from predicting depth from scratch, as the scale is already modeled by the camera output.

B.1. Ablations with ViT backbone
