Implementation Details:

The proposed approaches are implemented based on Monodepth2, maintaining its experimental settings. The depth CNN is a fully convolutional encoder-decoder network with a 640x192 input/output resolution. The Pose CNN is a standard CNN with a fully connected layer for regressing 6-DoF relative camera motion. Both networks use a ResNet18 backbone pretrained on ImageNet. For depth estimation, 2 nearby frames (S = {t-1, t+1}) and pair-input Pose are used. For ego-motion estimation, experiments include all-input Pose CNN with nearby 4 frames (S = {t -2, t -1, t + 1, t + 2}) and 2 frames (S = {t -1, t + 1}).

Hyper-parameters e, l, and e are set to 1, 0.001, and 0.5, respectively. The factor f for the weighted multi-scale scheme is set to 0.25. DiPE is trained for 20 epochs using Adam. DiPE uses a batch size of 16, consuming 9 hours on a single Titan Xp, compared to Monodepth2's 12 hours. DiPE's initial learning rate is 10-4, divided by 5 after 15 and 18 epochs, while Monodepth2 divides by 10 after 15 epochs. Reduced errors from outlier masking and gradual learning rate decrease aid DiPE's convergence. Monodepth2 uses uniform intrinsic parameters, approximating the principal point to the image center and averaging focal length. Calibrated intrinsic parameters are used for each training sample, with horizontal principal point coordinates flipped during horizontal flips in data augmentation.

DiPE: Deeper into Photometric Errors for Unsupervised Learning of Depth and Ego-motion from Monocular Videos

Unsupervised learning of depth and ego-motion from unlabelled monocular videos uses photometric errors between target and synthesized views as loss. This avoids expensive ground truth used in supervised methods. Despite progress, occlusion and scene dynamics cause issues. This paper proposes manipulating photometric errors to address these difficulties. A statistical technique masks invisible or non-stationary pixels in the photometric error map, preventing network misleading. This outlier masking approach improves depth estimation for objects moving opposite to the camera. Previous works have not adequately considered these scenarios, which are risky for applications like autonomous driving. An efficient weighted multi-scale scheme reduces artifacts in predicted depth maps. Experiments on the KITTI dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of these approaches, achieving state-of-the-art performance in both depth and ego-motion estimation.

Depth and ego-motion estimation is crucial for Simultaneous Localization And Mapping (SLAM). Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE) is used in applications like autonomous mobile robotics and AR/VR. Tracking 6-DoF camera motion is also vital. Traditional supervised methods require costly ground truth, limiting generalization. Unsupervised learning from monocular videos offers a more generalizable solution.

Unsupervised learning models typically consist of two networks: one for depth map prediction and another for motion estimation between temporally adjacent views. Using network outputs, the target view can be reconstructed from adjacent source views via image warping. The resulting photometric loss serves as the supervisory signal for learning. However, occlusion and scene dynamics disrupt image reconstruction, leading to incorrect supervision that harms network learning.

Figure 1 illustrates the detrimental effects of occlusion and dynamics. (a) Occlusion: Point P visible in camera view Ct is occluded in Ct+1. To achieve photometric consistency, P is matched to P' instead of Q, resulting in shorter depth estimation for P' (Q') and foreground object blur. (b) Co-directional motion: If point M moves forward with the camera C (from t-1 to t), it is likely estimated with farther depth (M't-1), creating 'dark holes'. (c) Contra-directional motion: When point M moves backward opposite to camera C (from t to t+1), it is estimated with shorter depth (M't+1).

The theory of minimizing between-view reconstruction errors impacting depth estimation of occluded regions and moving objects is shown in Figure 1. Many methods have addressed occlusion and dynamics with considerable improvement. For example, 'dark holes' caused by co-directionally moving objects have been tackled [2, 3, 4]. However, latest models show significant underestimation of depth for contra-directionally moving objects, as seen in Figure 4. This inaccuracy has not been previously reported and poses risks in applications like autonomous driving, where underestimating oncoming car distances could lead to unnecessary braking or avoidance maneuvers.

The final loss is a combination of photometric losses, smoothness loss, and cross-entropy loss:
$J_{total}^t = J_{ce}^t + \beta J_{sm}^t + \begin{cases} J_{phm}^t & \Lambda_t < \theta_{\Lambda} \\ J_{ph}^t & \text{else} \end{cases}$

$J_{ph}^t$, $J_{phm}^t$, and $J_{sm}^t$ are computed only on training images for depth estimation, while $J_{ce}^t$ is computed only in the segmentation domain. The weighting between segmentation and depth losses occurs during the backward pass.

Network Topology: An encoder-decoder architecture with skip connections is used, based on [20]. An Imagenet pretrained ResNet18 encoder is employed for comparability with existing work. The depth head has a sigmoid output $\sigma_{t,i}$, converted to a depth map by $1/(a\sigma_{t,i}+b)$, where $a$ and $b$ constrain depth values to [0.1, 100]. The segmentation decoder uses the same architecture as the depth decoder, with the last layer having $S$ feature maps converted to class probabilities by a softmax function. The pose network has the same architecture as in [20].

Training Aspects: Images are resized to 640x192 for depth estimation training (other resolutions like 416x128 and 1280x384 are evaluated). For semantic segmentation, images are randomly cropped to the same resolution. Zero-mean normalization is applied to RGB images for the ResNet encoder. Input images undergo augmentations: horizontal flipping, random brightness (+-0.2), contrast (+-0.2), saturation (+-0.2), and hue (+-0.1). Photometric losses are calculated on images without color augmentations. Loss is computed on four scales as in [20]. Gradient scaling from (6) is applied at encoder-decoder connections with a scale factor $\lambda = 0.1$. The fraction $\epsilon$ of images where photometric loss is not masked is set to 0 after 30 epochs and increases linearly to 1 by the last epoch. DC object classes $S_{DC}$ include all human and vehicle categories. Models are trained for 40 epochs using the Adam optimizer with batch sizes of 12 (single-task) and 6 (multi-task). Task-specific dataset batches are concatenated, passed through the encoder, then disconnected for respective decoders. The learning rate is initially 10-4, reduced to 10-5 after 30 epochs. Training only depth estimation is denoted "SGDepth only depth"; training both is "SGDepth full".

Databases: One dataset is used for semantic segmentation training (Cityscapes), and different subsets of the KITTI dataset are used for self-supervised depth estimation training. Depth estimation results are compared by training and evaluating on the Eigen split of KITTI, excluding static scenes. The single image depth prediction Benchmark split from KITTI is also used. For joint depth and segmentation prediction, the KITTI split defined by [18] is utilized. The number of training images may deviate from original definitions due to the need for preceding and succeeding images for depth estimation training.

Evaluation Metrics: Depth estimation is evaluated using four error metrics: absolute relative error (Abs Rel), squared relative error (Sq Rel), root mean squared error (RMSE), and logarithmic root mean squared error (RMSE log).

Depth is evaluated using absolute relative error (Abs Rel), squared relative error (Sq Rel), root mean squared error (RMSE), and logarithmic root mean squared error (RMSE log). Three accuracy metrics are computed: the fraction d of predicted depth values within a specified ratio (1.25, 1.252, 1.253) of ground truth. For the Benchmark split, scale-invariant logarithmic RMSE and inverse depth RMSE (iRMSE) are used. Median scaling is applied to predicted depths following [71]. Semantic segmentation is evaluated using mean intersection over union (mIoU) [13] with classes defined in [9].

The system uses two decoder heads: one for depth and one for segmentation. The segmentation decoder is trained in a source domain supervised by $y_{t,s}$ using (5). The depth decoder is trained in a target domain under self-supervision according to (3) and (4). For mini-batches containing data from both domains, gradients from separate decoders are propagated to the shared encoder. Instead of scaling loss functions as in other approaches, gradients are scaled when they reach the encoder. The total gradient $g_{total}$ propagated to the encoder is calculated as:
$g_{total} = (1 -\lambda) g_{depth} + \lambda g_{seg}$. (6)

Moving DC objects can contaminate the photometric error. This is addressed by masking regions with potentially moving DC objects. This is done by calculating a DC object mask $\mu_t$ from segmentation masks. The projected semantic mask $m'_{t\rightarrow t}$ is calculated by assigning the value of the closest pixel from $m'_{t}$ to the pixels of $m'_{t\rightarrow t}$.
$m'_{t\rightarrow t} = near(m'_{t}, u_{t\rightarrow t'}, u_{t'}) $. (7)
The DC object mask $\mu_t \in \{0, 1\}^{H \times W}$ is defined by its pixel elements:
$\mu_{t,i} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } m_{t,i} \notin S_{DC} \land m'_{t\rightarrow t,i} \notin S_{DC} \text{ for all } t' \in T' \\ 0 & \text{else} \end{cases}$ (8)
This mask contains 0 at each pixel position $i$ belonging to a DC object in any of the three frames, and 1 otherwise. A semantically-masked photometric loss $J^{phm}_t$ is defined, which only considers non-DC pixels:
$J^{phm}_t = \mu_t \odot min_{t' \in T'} (\alpha/2 (1 - SSIM(x_t, x'_{t\rightarrow t})) + (1 - \alpha) |x_t - x'_{t\rightarrow t}|)$. (9)
The mask from the auto-masking technique is also considered.

To detect non-moving DC objects, a measure is used to determine if a DC object is in motion. This is based on the consistency between the warped semantic mask in the target image $m'_{t\rightarrow t}$ and the semantic mask $m_t$ in the target image. The intersection over union for dynamic object classes is measured:
$\Lambda_{t,t'} = \frac{\sum_{i \in I} \kappa_{t,t',i}}{\sum_{i \in I} \nu_{t,t',i}}$, with
$\kappa_{t,t',i} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } m_{t,i} \in S_{DC} \land m'_{t\rightarrow t,i} \in S_{DC} \\ 0 & \text{else} \end{cases}$,
$\nu_{t,t',i} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } m_{t,i} \in S_{DC} \lor m'_{t\rightarrow t,i} \in S_{DC} \\ 0 & \text{else} \end{cases}$. (10)
$\Lambda_{t,t'} \in [0, 1]$ signals perfect alignment and no moving DC objects if it equals 1, while a value of 0 indicates a high share of moving DC objects. If two frames at times $t' \in T' = \{t-1, t+1\}$ are considered, the mean value $\Lambda_t$ of all $\Lambda_{t,t'}$ is used. A threshold $\theta_\Lambda \in [0, 1]$ is defined, above which an image is considered static.

Learning from non-moving DC objects involves calculating $\Lambda_t$ for each image and choosing $\theta_\Lambda$ such that a fraction $\epsilon \in [0, 1]$ of the images is trained without the semantically-masked photometric loss. The final loss $J^{total}_t$ is a combination of the photometric losses (9) and (3), the smoothness loss (4), and the cross-entropy loss (5):
$J^{total}_t = J^{ce}_t + \beta J^{sm}_t + \begin{cases} J^{phm}_t & \text{if } \Lambda_t < \theta_\Lambda \\ J^{ph}_t & \text{else} \end{cases}$. (11)

The ground truth depth labels cover only the bottom two-thirds of the image, failing to capture traffic signs and lights positioned above this zone. Our approach enhances learned depth for distant objects (DC objects), particularly pedestrians and cyclists, resulting in sharper visibility in depth maps. This improvement is attributed to our semantic masking technique, which leverages frames with stationary DC objects for depth learning.

We perform an ablative analysis on PackNet's architectural components to study performance improvements, as depicted in Table 4. The base architecture, without packing and unpacking blocks, already shows significant results.

During training, all four inverse depth output scales are used for loss calculation. At test time, only the final output scale is used, resized to the full ground-truth depth map resolution using nearest neighbor interpolation.

The Pose Network uses the architecture from [53] without the explainability mask, as it did not improve results. It comprises 7 convolutional layers followed by a 1x1 convolutional layer. The input is the target view $I_t$ and context views $I_s$, and the output is the set of 6 DOF transformations between $I_t$ and $I_s$ for $s \in S$.

**Depth Estimation Performance**

We report the performance of our monocular depth estimation method for longer distances, enabled by the new DDAD dataset. Depth estimation results on DDAD for training and evaluation, considering cumulative distances up to 200m, are shown in Fig. 5 and Table 2. Fig. 6 presents results for different depth intervals calculated independently. Our PackNet-SfM approach significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art [19] based on the ResNet family, with the performance gap increasing at larger distances.

We also evaluate depth predictions on KITTI using metrics from [14]. Results for original depth maps [14] and accumulated depth maps [42] are summarized in Table 3, with qualitative performance illustrated in Fig. 7. Unlike previous methods [6, 19] that modify the training objective, our PackNet architecture improves performance and sets a new state of the art for self-supervised monocular depth estimation.

Further improvement is achieved by incorporating unlabeled videos, such as the CityScapes dataset (CS+K) [9]. Consistent with [39], we observe improved performance at higher image resolutions, attributed to the network's ability to preserve and process spatial information end-to-end. Our best results, achieved with more unlabeled data and higher resolution inputs, are comparable to semi-supervised [29] and fully supervised [15] methods.

**Scale-Aware Depth Estimation Performance**

Self-supervised monocular methods [19, 34, 53] typically evaluate depth by scaling estimates to the median ground-truth from LiDAR. In Section 3.2, we propose recovering metric scale by imposing a loss on the magnitude of the pose network's translation output. Table 3 shows that this weak velocity supervision generates scale-aware depth models with performance similar to unscaled counterparts, without requiring ground-truth depth scaling or velocity information at test time. To study PackNet's performance improvements, an ablative analysis was performed on its architectural components. The base architecture, without packing and unpacking blocks, provides a strong baseline for monocular depth estimation. Incorporating packing and unpacking enhances performance, particularly with more 3D convolutional filters, leading to state-of-the-art results.

Generalization Capability: PackNet's generalization performance was investigated to demonstrate learning of transferable discriminative features rather than memorization of training data. Conclusion: PackNet, a novel convolutional network architecture for self-supervised monocular depth estimation, utilizes symmetrical, detail-preserving packing and unpacking blocks to compress and decompress high-resolution visual information for fine-grained predictions. Trained solely on unlabeled monocular videos, PackNet surpasses existing self- and semi-supervised methods and competes with fully-supervised methods, while also operating in real-time. Its enhanced generalization to different datasets and unseen environments, without ImageNet pretraining, is notable, particularly for longer depth ranges up to 200m on the DDAD dataset. Furthermore, by incorporating weak velocity information during training, PackNet becomes scale-aware, producing metrically accurate depth maps from single images.

4. PackNet: 3D Packing for Depth Estimation
Standard convolutional architectures use aggressive striding and pooling to increase their receptive field size, potentially decreasing model performance for tasks requiring fine-grained representations. Similarly, traditional upsampling strategies fail to propagate and preserve sufficient details at the decoder layers to recover accurate depth predictions. In contrast, we propose a novel encoder-decoder architecture, PackNet, that introduces new 3D packing and unpacking blocks to learn to jointly preserve and recover important spatial information for depth estimation. This aligns with recent observations that information loss is not a necessary condition to learn representations capable of generalizing to different scenarios. Progressive expansion and contraction in a fully invertible manner, without discarding "uninformative" input variability, has been shown to increase performance in a wide variety of tasks. We first describe the different blocks of our proposed architecture, and then show how they are integrated together in a single model for monocular depth estimation.

4.1. Packing Block
The packing block starts by folding the spatial dimensions of convolutional feature maps into extra feature channels via a Space2Depth operation. The resulting tensor is at a reduced resolution, but this transformation is invertible and lossless. Next, we learn to compress this concatenated feature space to reduce its dimensionality to a desired number of output channels. 2D convolutions are not designed to directly leverage the tiled structure of this feature space. Instead, we propose to first learn to expand this structured representation via a 3D convolutional layer. The resulting higher dimensional feature space is then flattened (by simple reshaping) before a final 2D convolutional contraction layer. This structured feature expansion-contraction, inspired by invertible networks, allows our architecture to dedicate more parameters to learn how to compress key spatial details that need to be preserved for high-resolution depth decoding.

4.2. Unpacking Block
Symmetrically, the unpacking block learns to decompress and unfold packed convolutional feature channels back into higher resolution spatial dimensions during the decoding process. The unpacking block replaces convolutional feature upsampling, typically performed via nearest-neighbor or with learnable transposed convolutional weights. It is inspired by sub-pixel convolutions, but adapted to reverse the 3D packing process that the features went through in the encoder. First, we use a 2D convolutional layer to produce the required number of feature channels for a following 3D convolutional layer. Second, this 3D convolution learns to expand back the compressed spatial features. Third, these unpacked features are converted back to spatial details via a reshape and Depth2Space operation to obtain a tensor with the desired number of output channels and target higher resolution.

Conclusion
MultiDepth is a method for introducing an auxiliary depth interval classification task to SIDE networks. Applied to SIDE in road scene understanding, extensive experiments show the benefits of posing SIDE as a multi-task problem with additional supervision from automatically derived ground-truth labels.

MultiDepth, with 32 classes for the auxiliary classification branch and learned task weighting, significantly outperforms single-task regression and classification baselines. MultiDepth achieved an SILog of 16.05 on the anonymous KITTI depth prediction test set, indicating the training strategy yields good overall results.

Source code for all experiments is publicly available.

Increasing the number of classes improves training stability and overall performance, with ncls >= 4 yielding only minor improvements. Using more classes than necessary does not significantly degrade results, but can produce a secondary output with lower quantization errors. Models with 4 <= ncls <= 64 achieved nearly identical validation results. ncls = 32 was selected for further experiments due to better convergence.

Learned multi-task weights improve the training process compared to equally weighted tasks or manually tuned weights. The baseline with fixed, equal weights converged to an unstable local minimum. Manually tuned fixed weights performed better than the equally weighted baseline but were significantly worse than learned dynamic weighting. Learned weights consistently outperformed manually tuned weights, demonstrating their effectiveness. Learning weights saves computation time and adds minimal parameters, even for multiple tasks.

Log-normalization of depth values using dataset-specific minimum and maximum depths (dmin, dmax) outperformed scaling from 0-256 m. This scaling approach spreads numerical precision effectively for the data and application. The optimal range may differ for other applications, such as indoor settings.

Training on larger patch sizes (256 x 256 px) outperformed smaller patches, especially with sparse ground truth data. This configuration yielded the best experimental results and was submitted to the KITTI depth prediction benchmark. Training with larger patches requires more memory and was conducted using parallelization with batch splitting.

The decoder for the classification task mirrors the regression branch structure. Shallow task-specific branches, with a high ratio of shared to individual parameters, encourage learning high-level features suitable for both tasks.

### Multi-Task Optimization
Joint training of both tasks involves combining individual losses ($L_{task}$) into a single multi-task objective ($L_{mt}$) for optimization. A simple approach is summing the losses: $L_{mt} = L_{reg} + L_{cls}$. To account for differing ranges and variances, weighting factors ($w_{reg}$, $w_{cls}$) are used: $L_{mt} = w_{reg} \cdot L_{reg} + w_{cls} \cdot L_{cls}$. Manual tuning of these weights as hyperparameters is tedious and may not adapt to training changes.

Automatic optimization of dynamic parameters is a promising approach. Existing methods weight tasks based on homoscedastic uncertainty or difficulty. We adopt the uncertainty-based weighting with parameters $w_{reg} = 0.5 \cdot \exp(-s^2_{reg})$ and $w_{cls} = \exp(-s^2_{cls})$, where $s_{task} = \log_e(\sigma^2_{task})$. We optimize for $s_{task}$ instead of $\sigma_{task}$ for numerical stability. To prevent minimizing $L_{mt}$ towards the trivial solution ($w_{reg} = w_{cls} = 0$), regularization terms ($r_{task} = 0.5 \cdot s_{task}$) are added, resulting in the final multi-task loss:
$L_{mt} = w_{reg} \cdot L_{reg} + r_{reg} + w_{cls} \cdot L_{cls} + r_{cls}$

### Experiments
A deep CNN was implemented and trained on a large road scene understanding dataset to evaluate the approach.

### Network Implementation
Given the shared feed-forward auto-encoder structure of SIDE and semantic segmentation networks, architectures are often shared. The auxiliary pixel-wise depth interval classification is a segmentation task, making well-performing deep CNNs for semantic segmentation suitable as a basis.

The PSPNet, with its pyramid pooling module for accumulating spatial context information, and the very deep ResNet-101 backbone for learning rich representations, are suitable. The network's encoder-decoder structure, using pyramid pooling and dilated convolutions, preserves high-resolution feature maps. PSPNet achieves state-of-the-art results on semantic segmentation datasets.

The network architecture was re-implemented in PyTorch and adapted for the multi-task approach. Parameters are shared through the ResNet encoder, accounting for approximately 50% of total parameters, enforcing learning of a common 2048-dimensional feature map representation. Task-specific components include the weights of pyramid pooling modules, subsequent blocks (convolution, batch normalization, ReLU, dropout), and final convolutional layers for output reshaping. Skip connections are used to retain spatial structure.

### Training and Validation Data
High robustness, redundancy, and accuracy in depth prediction are critical for autonomous driving. Multi-Depth is designed to meet these conditions, leading to its selection for training.

A common and robust representation for both tasks is learned by sharing a major part of the network weights. The encoder part, expected to learn a rich input data representation, should be shared to encourage this behavior. Decoders, containing few layers, extract and reshape task-specific information from the shared encoded features. State-of-the-art architectures often use very deep classification networks as encoders for deep feature extraction, which account for the majority of parameters.

**2.1 Efficient Optimization of Depth in Log-Space**

In autonomous driving, small errors in distance estimates for nearby objects can be fatal. Distances for faraway objects require lower accuracy. This can be addressed by estimation in non-linear space. Modern CNN-based SIDE methods use sophisticated loss functions to incorporate these desired properties. The scale invariant logarithmic error (SILog) is commonly used for scoring depth estimation results:

SILog(D, D) = 1/n (log di - log di)2 - 1/n2 ((log di - log di))2

where n is the number of depth values, D is the ground-truth depth, and D = (di) are the predicted depth maps. Extensive loss functions often yield superior results over basic ones like Mean Squared Error (MSE), which are computationally less expensive but may not directly optimize the final objective, acting as a reasonable proxy.

To overcome the limitations of both approaches, computationally expensive operations are relocated to data pre-processing. Parallel pre-loading of batches allows for more direct objective optimization while maintaining speed and efficiency. Depth values d are transformed to normalized log-space during data loading. With globally defined upper and lower boundaries dmin and dmax, the transformed depth is calculated as:

dlog = loge(d - dmin + 1) / loge(dmax - dmin + 1)

**2.2 Regression of Depth Values**

Task-specific decoders are added to extract information from encoder features. For the main regression task, the decoder directly predicts values in normalized log-space. Few network layers are expected to suffice for condensing and reshaping information along all feature map dimensions, given the rich encoder representation.

**2.3 Classification of Depth Intervals**

The auxiliary task of classifying discrete depth ranges requires corresponding target labels. To partition the continuous depth space, a number of intervals ncls is set. A relatively low number of classes ensures stable convergence while preserving enough detail to support the regression branch. Unlike methods using 80 intervals for ordinal regression, this approach uses classification to support the regression branch. Trading high quantization errors for stable convergence and robust performance is desirable. Following the concept of non-linearly scaled depth estimation and existing approaches, intervals are uniformly distributed in normalized log-space.

Apart from different target labels and a change in output feature dimension from one to ncls, the classification decoder closely resembles the regression branch structure. Keeping task-specific branches shallow maintains a high ratio of shared vs. individual parameters.

The learning rate a is a crucial hyperparameter. Following Smith, training was run for few iterations with an increasing learning rate. Starting from minuscule learning rates and exponentially increasing them to high values covered the full range of realistic a with only 250 optimization steps. Repeating this with different starting a and exponential scheduler parameters yielded an a vs. Lmt diagram. Four typical intervals of a were observed:
- a < 10-6: Stagnation of Lmt.
- 10-6 < a < 10-3: Decrease of Lmt, the desired range.
- a > 10-1: Lmt diverges.
Learning rates in the second interval were deemed suitable, and a = 10-4, close to the steepest descent of Lmt, was selected. Ablation studies were conducted to evaluate the approach with learned and dynamic weighting between depth estimation tasks. Training was performed from scratch without pre-trained weights for the ResNet encoder on a desktop with a single NVIDIA GeForce 1080Ti GPU, taking approximately 5 days.

For a baseline, the regression branch was trained without the classification branch. Single-task results improved initially but diverged after 105 iterations. Training and Validation Data
Predicting depth with high robustness, redundancy, and accuracy is crucial for autonomous driving. Multi-Depth was trained and evaluated on road scene images. The KITTI dataset, a comprehensive resource for road scene understanding, provides ground-truth for relevant tasks. The KITTI depth prediction dataset includes sparse point clouds from LiDAR sensors, with approximately 86,000 training samples. Ground-truth depth values are available for about 12% of pixels per image on average, dropping to 0.8% for some samples. Depth measurements exhibit unequal spatial distribution, with a notable lack of data in the upper image regions.

The model was trained on the full training set and validated on the 1000 images from the "val_selection_cropped" set. Final results were scored on the official KITTI depth prediction benchmark to evaluate performance against the state of the art.

Data Augmentation and Scaling
Input images were preprocessed using random cropping to resolutions between 128x128 px and 256x256 px. Smaller crop sizes resulted in more images with insufficient ground-truth information. Image scaling was avoided to leverage the network's fully-convolutional nature during inference, ensuring object scale consistency. Horizontal flipping was applied as data augmentation, improving results despite systematic differences in road scenes.

Depth values were scaled using Equation (2) with dmin = 2 m and dmax = 125 m, following the training dataset's depth distribution. The lower bound was set tightly to preserve accuracy in the lower normalized log-space, while the upper bound was more generous to accommodate higher depth values with minimal accuracy impact. Class labels for the classification branch were generated by binning scaled depth values into equally spaced intervals in normalized log-space, defined by dcmin and dcmax. Setting dcmin > dmin and dcmax < dmax simplified the auxiliary task, aiding its training.

Training Procedure
Given the sparse ground-truth data, a sparse MSE loss was implemented for the regression task and a sparse SoftMax cross-entropy loss for the classification task. The multi-task loss was constructed as presented in Equation (3). Weighting parameters for the multi-task loss (sreg and scls) were initialized to 1 and optimized with network parameters, consistent with findings on parameter robustness. Batch and patch sizes are interdependent due to GPU memory constraints; larger patches are preferred due to ground-truth sparsity.

Post-processing:
To address missing data on the left side of the disparity map due to occlusions, we employ a post-processing method inspired by Godard et al. [15]. At test time, for a given image I, we also infer the depth of its horizontally mirrored version, m(I). These two disparity images are then combined using a weighting function.

Discussion: Comparison with Godard et al. [15]
Differences in design between our approach and Godard et al. [15] are significant.

Similar loss, different components:
Godard et al. average predictions for two views, similar to our method. However, their predictions are not equivalent; both originate from the left view, with the right view serving only as supervision. In contrast, we provide inputs from both views simultaneously, treating them equally. This dual-input approach provides the network with more data, and each predicted disparity map is created independently from its corresponding image.

Siamese Network vs. Data Augmentation:
Our approach uses a Siamese network. Godard et al. [15] train a single input network on the left image, using the right image for supervision, and separately on flipped images with roles switched. This differs from our dual-input Siamese network.
1. Simultaneous backpropagation between branches in our dual-input network provides information unavailable in single-view training.
2. Including both left and right images as input compensates for occlusions and limited field-of-view.

Figure 3 compares the right disparity map from Godard et al. [15] to ours. Their output is blurry and lacks detail and contours, which can be attributed to their uncertainty regarding the right image, creating an asymmetry between dl and dr. Our predictions for both left and right disparities are fine-grained. The left-right consistency of our loss relies on accurate predictions of both, compelling the network to learn to predict the right disparity map as accurately as possible to minimize loss.

Reversing disparity directions:
While disparity directions can be reversed (dl = xl - xr and dr = xr - xl = -dl), this does not account for boundary effects seen in Figure 3. We anticipate boundary artifacts in left (right) disparities due to missing data. Furthermore, information distribution differs for left and right images (Il  Ir) due to camera positions. Our network is designed with a bias towards left images, but by exploiting symmetry and flipping right images, we assume Il ~ m(Ir). This allows us to avoid bias and use the same network for both.

Siamese networks double training time, but net throughput is the same as a single network trained separately on both images, as two training images are processed per step. Weight sharing also makes memory consumption unaffected.

3.2. Network Architecture

The network architecture is based on DispNet, with modifications similar to those described by Godard et al. ResNet and VGG architecture variants are used.

The network consists of an encoder-decoder pair with skip connections. These connections help overcome data loss during down-sampling while leveraging the benefits of a deep network.

The network produces multi-scale disparity maps: $d_1^{view}, \dots, d_4^{view}$, where $view$ represents either $l$ (left) or $r$ (right) for stereo pairs. Lower resolution disparity predictions are concatenated with previous decoder layer outputs and corresponding encoder outputs via skip connections. The concatenated results are then fed into the next scale of the network. A bilinear sampler, as used in [23], warps each disparity map and image onto its counterpart, enabling end-to-end back-propagation and learning.

3.3. Loss Function

A multi-scale loss is defined, related to one proposed previously. The single-scale loss is:
$L_s = \alpha_{im}(L_l^{im} + L_r^{im}) + \alpha_{tv}(L_l^{tv} + L_r^{tv}) + \alpha_{lr}(L_l^{lr} + L_r^{lr})$ (1)
The components of Eq. (1) average prediction errors from both left and right views. This differs from Garg et al., who consider single-view predictions, and Godard et al., who average two non-equivalent predictions.

The total loss is the sum over four scales:
$L = \sum_{s=1}^{4} L_s$ (2)
Using only the loss for the highest resolution scale resulted in lower accuracy compared to combining multiple scales.

An additional modification to the loss, Eq. (2), compared to previous work [15] is the use of a total variation component instead of their disparity smoothness term, which improved disparity results. The terms in Eq. (1) are detailed below.

Image Loss: Zhao et al. found that combining L1 loss with structural similarity (SSIM) loss [51] yields better results for image restoration. This loss function is also suitable for depth estimation [15, 54]. Unlike previous work [15] that used an average pooling version of SSIM, the original SSIM with a Gaussian kernel is used to improve metric localization.
SSIM is defined as:
$SSIM(x, y) = \frac{(2\mu_x\mu_y + c_1)(2\sigma_{xy} + c_2)}{(\mu_x^2 + \mu_y^2 + c_1)(\sigma_x^2 + \sigma_y^2 + c_2)}$ (3)
where $x$ and $y$ are equal-sized windows in the two images. $\mu_x, \mu_y, \sigma_x, \sigma_y$ are the mean and variance of $x$ and $y$, and $\sigma_{xy}$ is their covariance. The image loss is measured as:
$L_l^{im} = \alpha \sum_{i,j} \frac{1 - SSIM(I_l^{ij}, \hat{I}_l^{ij})}{2} + (1 - \alpha) \|I_l^{ij} - \hat{I}_l^{ij}\|$ (4)

Left-Right Consistency Loss: A constraint on the left-right consistency of estimated disparity images improves results [15]. Left-right consistency is introduced to the loss as a self-supervised feedback mechanism:
$L_l^{lr} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i,j} |d_l^{i,j} - d_r^{i,j + d_l^{i,j}}|$ (5)

Total Variation Loss: A total variation loss promotes smoothness in estimated disparity maps and acts as a regularization term:
$L_{tv}(d) = \sum_{i,j} |d_{i+1,j} - d_{i,j}| + |d_{i,j+1} - d_{i,j}|$ (6)
Weighting this loss with image gradients, as suggested in [15], was found to emphasize disparity gradients in undesirable areas like windows and walls, where objects should have uniform depth.

3.4. Post-processing

The left side of the disparity map often lacks data due to occlusions. A post-processing method, based on a suggestion from [23], is used to address this.

Our method is self-supervised. It achieves comparable accuracy to supervised methods and outperforms provided supervised baselines. Our method is also faster than previous methods.

To test generalization, we evaluate on the Make3D dataset. We use a model trained only on Cityscapes data, as it is higher resolution and contains similar scenes. We take a central crop of images to match Cityscapes aspect ratio.

The Make3D test set has 134 single-view RGB and depth image pairs. We use C1 error measures, ignoring pixels where depth is larger than 70 meters:
- Squared relative error (Sq Rel): $\frac{1}{T}\sum_{i}^{T}\frac{(dgt_i -dp_i )^2}{dgt_i}$
- Absolute relative error (Abs Rel): $\frac{1}{|T|}\sum_{i}^{T}\frac{dgt_i -dp_i }{dgt_i}$
- Root-mean squared error (RMSE): $\sqrt{\frac{1}{|T|}\sum_{i}^{T}(dgt_i -dp_i )^2}$
- log10 error: $\frac{1}{|T|}\sum_{i}^{T}log10(dgt_i ) -log10(dp_i )$

In these measures, $dgt_i$ is ground truth depth and $dp_i$ is predicted depth. Results are reported in Table 3, with qualitative results in Figure 6. Conclusions:
We propose a self-supervised monocular depth estimation method. It trains on stereo image pairs and applies to single images at test time. No depth information or supervisory data is needed during training; the system is fully self-supervised. We achieve state-of-the-art results on challenging datasets by better utilizing stereo input. Our key contribution is symmetrically handling left and right images by mirroring the right image.

We also make technical contributions, including a Siamese network with weight sharing. This halves model size, using only one network branch at runtime for single-view input. We further define a loss function that better represents our model's design.

An extension is to test our method in stereo rather than monocular settings, as it can be applied to stereo pairs. This ability to process monocular and stereo views is similar to the human visual system.

A disparity map is generated. This map is then used to inverse warp the right image, and reconstruction loss is measured. Our approach is similar to Godard et al. [15], but we use a specially crafted Siamese network for better training data utilization.

Our method also relates to Kuznietsov et al. [30], who also use two networks. Key differences include our use of weight sharing between two networks, reducing model size and enabling monocular settings at test time. Unlike their method, which uses depth information as a semi-supervisory signal, our method is completely self-supervised, requiring no depth or other labels. Our results nearly match theirs.

Some methods incorporate both depth and pose estimation [54, 57]. We focus solely on depth estimation and outperform these methods. Other work [29, 38, 53] uses self-supervision for depth extraction from monocular video, whereas we do not assume sequential data.

Siamese networks, first suggested by Bromley et al. [5], have been used for various tasks like metric learning [6] and recognition [27]. Some recent supervised depth estimation methods [25, 37] use Siamese networks, assuming stereo vision for both training and testing.

**3. Our approach**
We train using rectified stereo image pairs acquired in a controlled setup with a known camera baseline. This allows conversion from disparities to depth. We assume rectified stereo pairs are reasonably available, as seen in several datasets [7, 12, 39].

We aim to learn mappings $\hat{d}_l = f(I_l)$ from an RGB image to a left disparity map and $\hat{d}_r = f'(I_r)$ to a right disparity map. This differs from [15], where the training problem is formulated as $(\hat{d}_l, \hat{d}_r) = f(I_l)$.

The functions $f()$ and $f'()$ must differ because inferring left disparity is distinct from inferring right disparity due to different relative image positions and assigned disparities. While separate networks could be trained, this prevents weight sharing and exploitation of the problem's inherent symmetry. We propose a method that uses both images symmetrically.

**3.1. Siamese architecture with mirroring**
To utilize training data symmetrically, we exploit the problem's symmetry. By horizontally flipping the right image ($I_r$) to get $m(I_r)$, we can treat it as a left image and apply the $f()$ function. To return to right disparity, another mirroring is needed: $f'(\cdot) = m(f(m(\cdot)))$. This modified architecture, presented in Figure 2, contrasts with previous approaches. Garg et al. [11] and Godard et al. [15] use a single input image during training, with Garg et al. only using the right image as supervision.

Our Siamese architecture takes both images simultaneously during training, treating them equally. This saves memory and allows information sharing between networks.

Both previous methods [11, 15] under-utilize the right view by not feeding it into the encoder-decoder architecture. The right image is only used as a reference signal for the reconstructed image $\hat{I}_l(\hat{d}_r) = \hat{I}_r$. Data augmentation can flip both images to present them separately.

Figure 2 illustrates system architecture comparisons. Garg et al. [11] use the right image solely for supervision. Godard et al. [15] favor the left image. Both use a single training input. Our Siamese network trains on image pairs equally by flipping the right image. Our loss combines errors from two predictions, treating both views and their predictions equally. At test time, only the dashed-line bounded area is used; other blocks are for training.

The approach can be applied to stereo pairs, enabling processing of both monocular and stereo views, similar to the human visual system. Future work will explore the use of video and pose estimation within the framework. Integrating the post-processing step into the network training architecture for better end-to-end learning is another area for development. The approach utilizes relatively small networks, making it suitable for deployment on mobile platforms.

The network is initially trained on the Cityscapes dataset and then fine-tuned for 30 epochs on KITTI training images. This approach maximizes training data exposure while facilitating domain adaptation to KITTI.

For optimization, the Adam optimizer is employed with parameters b1 = 0.9, b2 = 0.999, and  = 10-8. A constant learning rate of l = 10-4 is used. The loss parameters from Eq. (2) are set as aim = 1.0, alr = 1.0, and atv = 0.001.

A batch size of eight is used for training. Data augmentation is performed through on-the-fly color, gamma, and brightness transformations. Training is conducted using the TensorFlow package on a Titan X GPU. The average test time per image is 73ms, including processing of the image and its mirrored version.

KITTI Eigen split:
The KITTI dataset comprises 42,382 rectified stereo pairs from 61 scenes, with most images measuring 1242 x 375 pixels. For comparability with prior work, the metrics and train/test splits defined by others are utilized.

The KITTI Eigen split includes 697 test images from 29 scenes, with an additional 32 scenes designated for training and evaluation. Ground truth depth data is generated by reprojecting 3D points from Velodyne laser scans onto the left image. It is important to note that depth data is sparse, available for only about 5% of pixels, and contains measurement noise from sensor rotation and vehicle movement.

The image crop defined by others is adopted for consistency with baseline methods. Predictions are rescaled to match the original image size using bilinear interpolation. While this is a common evaluation practice, concerns have been raised about its methodology. For completeness, results are provided for this protocol, but a more appropriate evaluation is suggested to be the KITTI single image prediction challenge, for which results are also presented.

Table 1 presents results on this dataset. The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art accuracy across most metrics, with a minor gap in RMSE and RMSE log compared to the best results. These metrics are considered less stable.

KITTI Single image depth benchmark:
The method is also evaluated on the recently released KITTI single image depth prediction challenge. This benchmark consists of 500 RGB test images for evaluation, with ground truth accessible only to dataset creators. Ground truth depth maps provided with the train/validation datasets are not used. Results are compared with existing public results, and qualitative examples are provided in Fig. 5.

This is a relatively new challenge with limited published results from supervised methods. While the proposed method does not always achieve the best results, it is the only self-supervised approach. Nevertheless, it demonstrates comparable accuracy to supervised methods and outperforms them.

Learn Stereo, Infer Mono: Siamese Networks for Self-Supervised, Monocular, Depth Estimation
Matan Goldman, Tal Hassner, Shai Avidan
Tel Aviv University, Israel, The Open University of Israel, Israel

Abstract
Self-supervised monocular depth estimation has advanced significantly. Most methods use stereo data during training but under-utilize it as only a reference signal. We propose a novel self-supervised approach that equally uses left and right images during training, yet can perform monocular depth estimation with a single input image at test time. Our Siamese network architecture has two twin networks, each predicting a disparity map from a single image. At test time, only one network infers depth. We achieve state-of-the-art results on the KITTI Eigen split benchmark and are the highest scoring self-supervised method on the KITTI single view benchmark. We also provide results on the Make3D benchmark, demonstrating generalization to new datasets.

1. Introduction
Single-view depth estimation is a fundamental computer vision problem with applications in autonomous driving, robotics, computational photography, and scene understanding. Although single-image depth estimation is ill-posed, humans can estimate depth from a single view using stereo vision, motion parallax, object familiarity, and perspective cues.

Classical computer vision methods, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have been used for monocular depth estimation. However, these methods are supervised and require large amounts of ground truth data. Obtaining ground truth depth data for realistic scenes is challenging and typically involves specialized equipment like LIDAR sensors.

To overcome this limitation, self-supervised approaches have emerged. These methods leverage the problem's intrinsic geometric properties for training monocular systems. While these methods assume both images are available during training, only one is used as input, with the second serving as a reference. Some methods, like Godard et al., improve accuracy by predicting both left and right disparity maps. However, estimating the right disparity using only the left image is prone to errors due to occlusions and missing information. Our method fully utilizes both images to learn single-image disparity estimation.

We propose a self-supervised approach similar to Godard et al. but exploit the symmetry of the disparity problem for effective deep models. Existing methods often train a single network to predict both left and right disparity maps from one image, which is problematic as crucial information from the right image is often occluded from the left viewpoint. Our approach involves flipping images vertically and training the network to predict a left disparity map. Right disparity maps are obtained by mirroring the right image, estimating disparity, and then mirroring the result back.

We use a deep Siamese network that learns to predict a disparity map from the left image and the flipped right image. This Siamese architecture allows learning each disparity map from its corresponding image. By mirroring the right image, predicting left and right disparity maps becomes equivalent. Consequently, both Siamese networks can be trained with shared weights, reducing computational cost and enabling single-image inference at test time.

FlowCLAS is a self-supervised normalizing flow-based framework leveraging vision foundation models (VFMs) for scene-level anomaly segmentation in robotics. It preserves VFM feature space, avoiding fine-tuning detrimental effects. Outlier Exposure and contrastive learning in the flow's latent space enhance anomaly detection. This dual approach, maintaining feature quality and introducing diverse pseudo-outliers, contributes to robust performance. FlowCLAS achieves state-of-the-art performance on the ALLO benchmark for space anomaly segmentation and competitive performance on road anomaly segmentation benchmarks compared to supervised approaches.

4. Experiments
This section details the experimental setup, benchmark results, and ablation studies for FlowCLAS.

4.1. Experimental setup

4.1.1. Datasets
Road anomaly segmentation experiments are conducted on the Fishyscapes (FS-L&F) subset and the Road Anomaly dataset. FS-L&F has 100 urban driving images with anomalies for validation. Road Anomaly provides 60 validation anomalous images. Cityscapes (2,975 images, 19 classes) is used for training.

The ALLO dataset is used for space anomaly segmentation, featuring 87,600 anomaly-free training images and 24,817 test images (anomalous and anomaly-free). Each image includes a 3-class mask: non-anomalous foreground, background, and anomalous regions.

For outlier exposure, objects from the COCO dataset are copy-pasted, selecting images with classes that do not visually overlap with test anomalies for Dout.

4.1.2. Evaluation metrics
Pixel-level performance is evaluated using two binary classification metrics: Area Under Precision Recall Curve (AUPRC) and False Positive Rate (FPR) at a True Positive Rate (TPR) of 95% (FPR95). FPR95 is prioritized for robotics applications where high TPR and minimal false positives are critical. AUPRC is important for imbalanced scenarios with small anomalous objects.

Implementation details:
FlowCLAS is applied post-hoc to features extracted by a frozen vision foundation model. DINOv2-L is utilized for feature extraction.
The normalizing flow is constructed with 8 and 16 blocks for space and road anomaly segmentation experiments, respectively. A cosine learning rate scheduler with linear warmup is employed, with a maximum learning rate of 1x10-5 and weight decay. The projection head reduces features to a dimensionality of C' = 256. The temperature parameter t is set to 0.10. FlowCLAS is trained for 10 epochs on the ALLO dataset and 600 epochs on Cityscapes, using a batch size of 32.
Code development is based on the Anomalib library. MMSegmentation is used to reimplement specific modules and baseline methods. RPL is reimplemented using DeepLabV3+ with a ResNet-101 backbone from MMSegmentation (denoted as RPL+ for the ALLO experiments).
A baseline, FastFlow+DINOv2-L, is established by reimplementing FastFlow with a DINOv2-L encoder to address the research gap in domain-agnostic unsupervised methods for scene-level anomaly segmentation.

Road anomaly segmentation results:
FlowCLAS achieves state-of-the-art performance across all metrics on both benchmarks among non-inlier label reliant methods. It demonstrates competitive performance against domain-aware methods that rely on inlier class labels, achieving the highest AUPRC score on Road Anomaly and second-best FPR95 scores on both datasets. These results are achieved without requiring labels for fine-tuning.
The domain-agnostic likelihood-based post-hoc approach, leveraging a vision foundation model, demonstrates excellent anomaly segmentation performance without the need for fine-tuning, highlighting its potential for applications where diverse labeled data is not available.

Space anomaly segmentation results:
The method's performance is evaluated on the space anomaly segmentation task using the ALLO benchmark. Comparisons include representative methods from industrial defect inspection (IDI) and medical imaging domains that do not require inlier labels, aligning with FlowCLAS. UNO and RPL are also benchmarked. IDI and medical imaging baseline methods generally underperform on ALLO anomalous images, likely due to their design for narrower feature distributions, making them less effective in handling complex scene changes.
FlowCLAS significantly outperforms FastFlow, the previous best performing method in AUPRC and FPR95 scores. FlowCLAS demonstrates superior accuracy in segmenting anomalous objects and enhanced robustness in challenging scenarios, such as low lighting or small object sizes.

3.2. Pseudo-anomalies with Outlier Exposure
Anomalous images are generated by pasting random objects from an auxiliary dataset into anomaly-free training images. The anomaly-free training dataset is Din = {xin}i|Din|, where x RHxW x3. Unlike previous approaches, this method assumes no pixel-level categorical labels. An auxiliary dataset is Dout = {(xouti, youti)}i|Dout|, where youti RHxW is a binary mask separating foreground objects from the background. Anomalous images are created by copy-pasting objects from Dout into Din using binary masks, resulting in a mixed dataset Dmix = {xmixi, ymixi}i|Dmix|.
The mixed image xmixi is computed as:
xmixi = (1 -ymi) xin + ymixi xout (3)
where ymixi RHxW is the resulting binary mask after randomly scaling the anomalous object and pasting it into a random location of the original image.

3.3. Normalizing flow for anomaly segmentation
A frozen pre-trained feature extractor, such as a vision foundation model, is denoted as fph : X RHxW x3 -X' RH'xW 'xC. A normalizing flow is denoted as fth : X' -Z RH'xW 'xC. The normalizing flow outputs 2D latent maps zmix, zout Z given a mixed image xmix and an outlier image xout:
zi = fth(fph(xi)), i {mix, out} (4)
The outlier image is provided to produce more outlier samples for the outlier sets described in Sec. 3.4.1.
The mapping fth(*) is implemented as a sequence of L invertible blocks: fth = f1th *f2th ** * * *fLth. Each block consists of invertible operations:
zl = Affine(RandPermute(Actnorm(zl-1))) (5)
where Actnorm is activation normalization, RandPermute is a random channel-wise permutation, and Affine is an affine coupling layer with 2D subnets.
The normalizing flow fth is trained to maximize the log-likelihoods of only non-anomalous features:
Lml = (y'mix -1) log pX'(x'mix) = (y'mix -1) [log pZ(zmix) + log det(zmix/x'mix)] (6)
where y'mix RH'xW ' is ymix downsampled to H' x W ' and zmix = fth(x'mix). zout is computed but not used for maximum likelihood training.
During training, the network models the feature distribution of a vision foundation model using a Multivariate Gaussian Distribution (MGD) in the latent space, characterized by mean u and diagonal covariance S. This allows for efficient computation of the exact likelihood map of feature maps, which can be used to obtain an anomaly score with a probabilistic interpretation.

3.4. Leveraging pseudo-outliers for enhanced separation in latent space
In the traditional maximum likelihood framework, normalizing flow networks are trained to assign high likelihood scores to inliers, assuming outlier features will naturally be projected far from inlier latent samples. This method combines Outlier Exposure with contrastive learning to explicitly encourage the density estimator to project outliers to regions of the latent space distant from inliers, enhancing the network's ability to distinguish anomalies from normal samples.

3.4.1. Projection to lower-dimensional space
Zmix denotes the set of all pixel-level latent vectors from Dmix: Zmix = {zmix = fth(fph(xmix))i,j} for all xmix  DmixoH',W'. Zout is similarly defined for Dout. The elements of Zmix and Zout are transformed into samples of a standard multivariate normal distribution, denoted as -z, using known parameters u and S. These sample vectors are processed through a projection head comprising a 1x1 convolutional layer and channel-wise L2 normalization. This projection maps them into a lower-dimensional space to enhance discriminative power and reduce redundancy for contrastive learning.

3.4.2. Self-supervision using supervised contrastive learning
Inlier and outlier anchor sets, Ain and Aout, are constructed by randomly sampling subsets of Zmix using the masks ymix. Similarly, sets Bin and Bood are derived from Zout. This sampling process ensures an equal number of samples in each set for class balance.

We investigate the effects of individual prompts by splitting the RA19 dataset into subsets of frames containing a specific OOD concept (known unknowns) and frames showing other OOD concepts but not the selected one (unknown unknowns). We measure VL4AD performance on the whole dataset and both subsets, with and without OOD prompting. AP and FPR on known unknowns subsets are generally better with OOD prompting, indicating our model retains open-vocabulary capabilities and can reject OOD objects. For unknown unknowns subsets, we observe statistically insignificant fluctuations around 1% in AP and FPR when applying different prompts. OOD prompts positively affect OOD detection on known unknowns while having a negligible impact on unknown unknowns. This is expected as OOD prompts increase ID class uncertainty only when corresponding OOD objects appear. We also experiment with OOD class names from RbA's outlier supervision dataset as prompts. Overlapping classes between RbA and RA19, such as cow and zebra, result in similar performance to previously used prompts. This highlights the flexibility and effectiveness of OOD prompting.

Compared to vision-only Mask2Former, VL4AD includes an additional text encoder. However, textual embeddings from ID semantic classes and OOD prompts are cached, avoiding further text encoder passes at test time. VL4AD is approximately 5% slower than vision-only ConvNext with Mask2Former on an NVIDIA A100. This slight difference is likely due to VL4AD's cosine similarities with text embeddings involving more parameters than the linear layers in vision-only Mask2Former.

Our VL4AD approach uses the FC-CLIP architecture, comprising frozen CLIP text and vision encoders paired with a Mask2Former (M2F) decoder. The model accepts visual inputs along with ID and optional OOD class prompts, providing pixel-wise uncertainty scores for anomaly detection.

We use max-logit prompt ensembling, originally devised to enhance generalization. Max-logit prompt ensembling significantly increases the model's sensitivity to OOD inputs by introducing concept lexical diversification and concretization in textual prompts. Lexical diversification includes synonyms and plural forms, while concretization involves decomposed concepts that align better with CLIP's pre-training. For example, the concepts {vegetation, tree, trees, palm tree, bushes} represent the class vegetation. Max-logit ensembling considers all alternative concepts for a given class k by replacing the term cos(vi, tk) with the maximum cosine similarity between visual embeddings vi and the textual embeddings of all l alternative text embeddings [t1k, . . . , tlk] for the k-th class:

max[cos(vi, t1k), cos(vi, t2k), ..., cos(vi, tlk)] (3)

Solely relying on maximum pixel-wise scores along the K-class dimension can lead to suboptimal performance due to high uncertainty at edge pixels between two ID classes, especially as the number of classes increases. To address this, we propose merging related ID classes into superclasses. This is achieved by concatenating the textual prompts of individual semantic classes as different alternative concepts within superclasses during testing, without retraining. Uncertainty of superclasses is then obtained using the max-logit fashion.

### Data- and Training-Free Outlier Supervision via OOD Prompting

Vision-language pre-training typically detects semantic OOD classes distinct from ID classes (far-OOD). However, near-OOD cases, where OOD classes closely resemble ID classes, are more challenging. For instance, in CityScapes, the OOD class caravan may appear visually similar to the ID class truck. Leveraging open-vocabulary capabilities, we introduce a new scoring function to better detect these near-OOD classes without additional training or data preparation. To integrate Q new OOD concepts at test time, mask classification scores ci from Eq. 1 are extended by Q additional terms cos(vi, t<0xE1><0xB5><0x8F>+1), ..., cos(vi, t<0xE1><0xB5><0x8F>+<0xE1><0xB5><0x8F>). Combining the first K channels of c [0, 1]Nx(K+<0xE1><0xB5><0x8F>) with mask prediction score s [0, 1]NxHxW, we obtain final uncertainty scores u RHxW. With this integration, OOD objects from these Q classes will (in most cases) be correctly assigned to their corresponding class. Without it, they would be mistakenly assigned to a similar ID class. If no OOD object is present, the impact of additional Q classes remains negligible. See Fig. 4 for illustration.

Visual embeddings $v_i$ combine visual features from the decoder's pixel-decoding part ($D_{vis-lang}$) and features directly obtained via mask pooling from the encoder ($E_{vision, vis-lang}$). Instead of summing these, FC-CLIP constructs a geometric ensemble of logits by computing cosine similarity between individual visual features and ID class textual embeddings. The final mask classification scores are given by:
$c_i(j) = \begin{cases} (c_{i, \text{in}}(j))^{(1-\alpha)} \cdot (c_{i, \text{out}}(j))^\alpha, & \text{if } j \in K \\ (c_{i, \text{in}}(j))^{(1-\beta)} \cdot (c_{i, \text{out}}(j))^\beta, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$
where $c_i(j)$ is the $j$-th element of $c_i$, $i = 1, \ldots, N$, and $N$ is the number of object queries. $\alpha, \beta \in [0, 1]$ balance predictions between in- and out-of-vocabulary classifiers for ID and OOD prompting classes.

To examine the relationship between mask classification features and OOD detection performance, experiments were conducted for VL4AD without OOD prompting, varying $\alpha$ from 0.0 to 1.0. $\alpha = 0.0$ means exclusive reliance on decoder-processed visual features, while $\alpha = 1.0$ means mask generation solely for CityScapes classes, with scores dependent entirely on raw vision encoder features.

The AP remained consistently high across RA19 and FS LaF datasets, significantly surpassing the vision-only variant. A notable variation in the false positive rate (FPR) on RA19 was observed. At $\alpha = 0.0$ (only in-vocabulary classifier), the model overfit to CityScapes training data. At $\alpha = 1.0$ (only out-of-vocabulary classifier), the model failed to learn effectively from CityScapes data, resulting in problematic uncertainty distribution and a significantly higher FPR. Settings $\alpha = 0.4$ and $\alpha = 0.6$ showed the best balance, indicating moderate fine-tuning on in-distribution data is essential for effective OOD detection. Improved performance was also observed with OOD prompting at $\alpha = 0.4$. Consequently, $\alpha = 0.4$ and $\beta = 0.8$ were used.

To mitigate overfitting, measures were taken on the vision and text sides. Random cropping with a ratio of 1.1 between original image size and crop was applied to input images. Textual prompts were constructed by combining prompt templates and alternative concepts. For each prompt, eight variants were created by applying 1% dropout to attention and feed-forward layers of the transformer-based text encoder prior to training. During training, these eight variants were sampled. At inference, dropout was disabled, and the normalized mean of textual embeddings with respect to prompt templates served as representative textual embeddings for each alternative concept.

The model was initially trained on the COCO-panoptic dataset for 50 epochs with a batch size of 16 and a learning rate of $10^{-4}$. Subsequently, it was fine-tuned on the CityScapes dataset for 10K iterations with a batch size of 8 and a learning rate of $2.5 \times 10^{-5}$, a setup consistent for both VL4AD and vision-only baselines. For the unfrozen vision-only variant, the learning rate of the encoder was reduced.

On RA19, approximately 2% of CityScapes pixels are incorrectly identified as OOD. With OOD prompting, this reduces to approximately 0.5%, demonstrating its effectiveness. On FS LaF, both variants misclassify 3% of CityScapes pixels at a recall of 0.9, using OOD prompts from RA19.

VL4AD achieves a recall of 0.9 on both RA19 and FS LaF while correctly identifying at least 97% of CityScapes pixels as ID. OOD prompting further enhances ID retention on RA19.

Limitations include VL4AD's reliance on CLIP's vision encoder, which struggles with small obstacles, leading to weak pixel-level performance on RO21. Enhancing CLIP's local representation capabilities for dense prediction tasks is a future direction. VL4AD also uses a concept dictionary and fixed prompt templates. Experiments with learnable prompts did not improve anomaly detection performance, potentially due to overfitting to limited semantic classes in CityScapes. Developing effective training strategies for learnable prompts in limited-class pixel-wise anomaly detection remains a challenge.

This work addresses pixel-wise anomaly detection by leveraging vision-language models, which are more OOD-aware due to broader pre-training. This contrasts with vision-only methods limited by standard training sets and reliant on outlier supervision. Max-logit prompt ensembling improves alignment between ID textual and visual embeddings. Class merging avoids high uncertainty on edge pixels between ID classes. A new scoring function tailored for vision-language models enables data- and training-free outlier supervision via textual prompts. VL4AD is evaluated on RA19, FS LaF, and SMIYC, comparing against methods like RbA and UNO. Experimental results show VL4AD is competitive with vision-only models but does not require additional data collection, labeling, and retraining. The strategy, including max-logit prompt ensembling, class merging, and OOD prompting, significantly improves performance and showcases vision-language models' capability in pixel-level anomaly detection.

**Conclusion:**

Robust performance in the presence of outliers is crucial for scene understanding applications. Previous dense prediction approaches often fail due to their reliance on pixel-level Out-of-Distribution (OOD) detection, neglecting correlations between neighboring pixels. This work shifts OOD detection from pixels to regions (mask-level), aggregating pixel-level evidence to increase the statistical power of anomaly scores. Performing OOD detection before ensembling decisions over masks further boosts performance. Injecting negative data into void content and extending the mask-based model for panoptic inference in the presence of outliers are also demonstrated. Experiments show that mask-level outlier detection significantly outperforms pixel-level counterparts and achieves state-of-the-art AP performance among methods not trained on real negative data. It also improves upon the previous state of the art in outlier-aware panoptic segmentation.

4.2. Outlier-aware panoptic segmentation on MS COCO
Mask-level outlier detection can be applied for panoptic segmentation. We consider a setup from a related work that relabels 20% of thing classes from COCO as void pixels during training. These classes include dining table, banana, bicycle, cake, sink, cat, keyboard, and bear. During inference, the model must classify all pixels from these classes into the dedicated anomalous thing class.

Outlier-aware performance is measured using standard metrics PQ, SQ, and RQ. Our models use a ResNet-50 backbone, consistent with previous work.

Mask-level training encourages all masks to refrain from encompassing void pixels. Our anomaly detectors are sensitive to the resulting lack of mask assignment. Therefore, our supervision intensity is similar to void-suppression. Our inference recovers the dense anomaly map by thresholding the mask-level anomaly score. We validate the threshold for 95% TPR in outlier detection on a held-out validation image. Each anomalous pixel is assigned to its preferred mask, and instances are formed by keeping all masks with more than 200 pixels.

Detecting outliers in mask-level predictions begins with recovering dense anomaly scores as mask-level uncertainty of the strongest mask. Using max-softmax as the uncertainty measure:

Closed-set semantic scores are viewed as ensembled outputs of per-mask classifiers, with mask assignments as weights. This score is denoted as Anomaly of Ensembled Mask-wide predictions (AEM).

Anomaly detectors are applied directly to mask-level classification scores. Evidence in each pixel is aggregated by its mask assignments m. This approach, Ensemble over Anomaly scores of Mask-wide predictions (EAM), relates directly to mask-level uncertainty. Quantifying mask-level uncertainty with maximum per-class probability yields a lower bound of the AEM score (6):
sEAM ood (x)[r, c] = X i mi[r, c] * (-max k=1...K Pi(Y = k|x)) <= -max k=1...K X i mi[r, c] * Pi(Y = k|x) (7)
The difference between AEM and EAM is most visible at semantic borders where adjacent masks lower pixel assignment confidence. EAM correctly outputs a lower anomaly score than AEM in these situations, reducing false positives in inlier pixels at semantic boundaries.

Performance enhancement with negative data is crucial for outlier detection and addresses feature collapse. For dense prediction, negative data is typically pasted over inlier training images, requiring an additional loss term in negative pixels. This approach requires no changes to the model or loss function.

Negative pixels are set to the void class ground truth, instructing masks to avoid them. This increases void content variety and penalizes masks that claim void pixels. Standard dense classifiers [14, 50] cannot train with negatives labeled as void due to per-pixel cross-entropy loss not computing in void pixels. This pasting procedure is specific for mask-level recognition. Training examples demonstrate that this supervision generalizes to outlier detection in real-world images.

Experiments explore the advantages of mask-level recognition in outlier-aware semantic segmentation.

Combining the proposed EAM outlier detector with negative supervision attains competitive results in outlier-aware semantic and panoptic segmentation. Further improvements can be obtained by combining the proposed approach with negative supervision. The resulting models set the new state of the art in outlier-aware segmentation on two tracks from the Segment Me If You Can (SMIYC) benchmark and adapted MS COCO.

2. Related work
The related work considers models for mask-level recognition tasks (Sec. 2.1) and segmentation in presence of outliers (Sec. 2.2).

2.1. Recognition of free-form regions
Early approaches to mask-wide recognition relied on class-agnostic bottom-up proposals. They aggregated handcrafted or convolutional features along the proposed regions and brought mask-wide decisions by classifying pooled representations. Mask-RCNN extends this approach by sharing features across detection of proposals and mask-wide classification, as well as by end-to-end training of all parameters. Recently, PointRend proposes to back-propagate the loss only through selected low-uncertainty predictions. This allows to increase Mask-RCNN resolution from 28x28 to 224x224 with a neglectable impact on the training footprint. Very recently, MaskFormer precludes dependence on bottom-up proposals by directly assigning pixels to masks that span arbitrary image regions. Its key component is a hypernetwork that produces the weights for two 1x1 convolutions that convert pixel-level embeddings into mask assignment scores and, subsequently, into semantic maps. This is the first architecture that succeeds to deliver competitive experimental performance on three dense recognition tasks: semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, and panoptic segmentation. Mask2Former further improves the mask hypernetwork by introducing a special kind of attention layer that promotes progressive focusing onto foreground pixels for a particular mask. Our work explores the Mask2Former performance in the context of outlier-aware segmentation and outlier-aware panoptic segmentation.

2.2. Segmentation in presence of outliers
Recognition in the wild involves test regions beyond the training taxonomy. Adequate models should reject the decision in such pixels. This can be carried out by restricting the shape of the decision boundary or by complementing the classifier with an anomaly detector. The decision boundary can be restricted by thresholding distance from the learned class centers in the embedding space. This can be further improved by employing a stronger classifier. Nevertheless, many of these approaches are bound to fail if unknown samples happen to map to the same features as the samples from the known classes. This occurrence is known as feature collapse.

Early approaches for extending discriminative predictions with OOD detection have been based on prediction confidence, input perturbations, density estimation and Bayesian uncertainty. Several studies point out that semantic anomalies may be especially hard to detect. A promising approach involves generating synthetic anomalies in tandem with the discriminative task. Further empirical improvements have been achieved by mimicking anomalies with negative training data. However, this may lead to over-optimistic performance estimates due to possible overlap with test anomalies.

Outlier detection is especially interesting in the dense prediction context due to important applications in robust scene understanding. However, straight-forward adaptations of image-wide approaches experience two important failure modes. First, they often fail to accurately localize anomalies in front of inlier backgrounds. Second, they are prone to false positives in inlier pixels with high entropy predictions that occur regularly at semantic borders. Hence, a large body of work proposes custom designs to alleviate these problems.

Partially anomalous images can be accounted for by learning on mixed-content images. Correlation between neighbouring pixels can be addressed by aggregating evidence through meta-classification or input preprocessing. Real training data can be avoided by fitting generative heads to pre-trained or jointly trained features. Another line of work trains on synthetic negatives corresponding to adversarial noise or samples of a jointly trained generative model. Finally, some approaches detect the discrepancy between the input and the resynthesised scene.

4.2 Main Results
Pixel-level Results. Our method significantly outperforms the baseline RbA and achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple datasets. While RPL+CoroCL achieves slightly better AuROC and FPR on the Fishyscapes Lost&Found dataset, SOTA improves the AuPRC by a significant margin of 5.5% compared to RPL+CoroCL. Furthermore, SOTA consistently outperforms RPL+CoroCL across all other datasets.

Component-level Results. Compared to RbA, our method achieves substantial improvements on RA-21, including a 5.58% increase in sIoU, an 18.31% boost in PPV, and a 14.67% gain in F1*. Similarly, on RO-21, our method yields an 8.00% improvement in PPV and a 9.55% increase in F1*. While Mask2Anomaly achieves a higher performance on RO-21, our approach surpasses it on RA-21, achieving a 0.88% improvement in sIoU and a 12.87% increase in F1*. Moreover, while ContMAV achieves higher PPV and F1* scores on RA-21, it does not report results on RO-21, whereas our approach consistently enhances performance across both datasets.

Qualitative Results. RPL tends to generate diffused predictions with substantial false positives, particularly along object boundaries and in areas outside the road region. Although RbA improves upon RPL by offering sharper delineation, it still suffers from incomplete segmentation and residual noise. In contrast, SOTA delivers more accurate and comprehensive segmentation of OOD objects while effectively suppressing extraneous pixel predictions beyond the road area. These qualitative findings underscore the advantages of our approach, which unifies attribute-aware feature learning and scene-guided context modeling to achieve a superior balance between precise anomaly localization and noise reduction.

4.3 Ablation Studies
SOTA Ablation Analysis. In configuration (a), no additional modules are applied, representing the baseline RbA output. In configuration (b), only the SG-PCA variant using the raw OOD prompt fusion (~y) is applied, effectively using RbA's anomaly score as the mask prompt input to SAM. Configuration (c) incorporates only the SFB along with mask decoder finetuning, thereby directly integrating the enhanced image features with the anomaly cues. In configuration (d), only the SG-PCA variant using the raw OOD prompt fusion (~y) is applied with fine-tuning. Configuration (e) applies SG-PCA with both the raw OOD prompt fusion (~y) and the road semantic prompt (y't); here, the dual cues help refine the spatial context, yielding a distinct performance pattern. Configuration (f) employs SG-PCA with the combination of the raw OOD prompt and the road-related OOD prompt fusion (~yt) with finetuning, demonstrating further improvement by incorporating contextual information that accounts for partial object extensions. In configuration (g), both SFB and SG-PCA (using ~y and ~yt) are integrated without finetuning the mask decoder, whereas configuration (h) activates both modules together with finetuning. Notably, configuration (h) achieves the highest performance, which yields a relative AuPRC gain and the lowest FPR on both RoadAnomaly and Fishyscapes Lost & Found. This indicates that the combined use of SFB and the SG-PCA variant employing both ~y and ~yt is crucial.
