4 Experiments
AMBERT is compared against baselines including fine-grained BERT and coarse-grained BERT, as well as alternatives AMBERT-Combo and AMBERT-Hybrid. Comparisons are made on benchmark datasets in Chinese and English. Experiments on alternatives serve as ablation studies for AMBERT. Ablation studies for regularization term l are in Appendix E.

4.1 Data for Pre-Training
For Chinese, a corpus of 25 million documents (57G uncompressed text) from Jinri Toutiao is used. For English, a corpus of 13.9 million documents (47G uncompressed text) from Wikipedia and OpenWeb-Text is used.

Chinese texts' characters are treated as fine-grained tokens. Word segmentation is performed on texts, and words are treated as coarse-grained tokens, using an n-gram model-based word segmentation tool.

Convolutional filters help words focus on their importance and relationships with neighboring words, allowing for simultaneous global and local dependency maintenance. Experiments showed that SesameBERT significantly improved performance on most GLUE tasks compared to BERT. SesameBERT also performed well on the HANS evaluation set, which diagnoses structural heuristic use, indicating it does not solely rely on heuristics. This implies the model is competitive across multiple downstream tasks.

Unsupervised pretraining in NLP initially relied on pretrained word vectors, which had limitations as they captured semantics without considering context. Contextualized word representations, such as ELMo, addressed this by using hidden states in LSTMs to extract context-sensitive representations. Generative pretraining used Transformer encoders but was unidirectional. BERT, using a masked language modeling task, achieved high performance but presented challenges in selecting the most appropriate pooling strategy due to varying information encoded in different layers.

The Squeeze and Excitation method, introduced by Hu et al. (2018), enhances representation quality by recalibrating features. Traditional convolutional neural networks treat channels equally. Squeeze and Excitation allows networks to use global information to emphasize important features and suppress less important ones.

Self-attention networks capture global dependencies regardless of distance. Our Gaussian-blurring method focuses on learning local contexts while retaining the ability to capture long-range dependencies. Localness modeling, previously a learnable Gaussian bias predicting a central position and dynamic window, was adapted. Instead of masking logit similarity, Gaussian bias was applied after the embedding layer through element-wise operations to improve model performance.

A study by McCoy et al. (2019) investigated whether neural networks adopt shallow heuristics instead of learning generalizations. In computer vision, object recognition models have been misled by contextual heuristics. In natural language inference, models might predict contradictory labels due to specific words like "not" appearing in training examples.

Models may learn to assume a label is contradictory whenever a negation word is contained in the premise but not the hypothesis. Whether a model scored well on a given test set because it relied on heuristics can be observed. For example, BERT performed well on MNLI tasks but poorly on the HANS dataset, suggesting the BERT model employs lexical overlap heuristics.

The MNLI dataset has three labels: Entailment, Neutral, and Contradiction. The HANS dataset translates instances labeled as Contradiction or Neutral into non-entailment, resulting in two labels: Entailment and Non-entailment. The HANS dataset targets three heuristics: Lexical overlap, Subsequence, and Constituent. This dataset measures progress and enables visualization of interpretable model shortcomings trained using MNLI.

Experiments were conducted using a batch size of 32, learning rates of 3e-5, and 3 epochs for all GLUE tasks. The SesameBERT model was fine-tuned across 9 downstream tasks. For each task, fine-tuning was performed with Gaussian blur kernel sigmas of 1e-2, 1e-1, 3e-1, and 5e-1, selecting the sigma with the most favorable performance on the dev set. Predictions were uploaded to the GLUE server for evaluation as GLUE datasets do not distribute labels for test sets. In most tasks, the proposed method outperformed the original BERT-Base model, with SesameBERT yielding improvements of 1.2% and 1.6% on the RTE and AX datasets, respectively. Experiments on GLUE datasets tested the effects of Gaussian blurring alongside BERT on the value layer and context layer. The performance of Gaussian blurring with respect to self-attention layers varied.

Gong et al. demonstrated that different layers vary in their abilities to distinguish and capture neighboring positions and global dependency between words. Weights learned from all layers indicated that a heavier weight represents greater importance. Lower layers, representing word embeddings deficient in context, may struggle to learn localness and may need to encode representations with global context. The results indicated that lower layers had lower accuracy.

Three ablation studies were performed. First, the performance of the method without blurring was examined, observing that Squeeze and Excitation aided the higher layer, suggesting higher layers benefit more than lower layers. Second, the effect of Gaussian blurring on the context layer was analyzed, revealing that the method with blurring achieved higher accuracy in lower layers. Capturing short-range dependencies among neighboring words in lower layers is assumed to be an effective strategy.

Gaussian blurring was analyzed for its effect on the context layer. Blurring achieved higher accuracy in lower layers, suggesting capturing short-range dependencies among neighboring words is effective. Even with self-attention models capturing long-range dependencies in higher layers, modeling localness remains helpful. SesameBERT performed poorly in lower layers but outperformed other methods in higher layers, indicating Squeeze and Excitation with Gaussian blurring aids self-attention models in capturing global information across all layers.

On the MNLI-m dataset, BERT achieved 84.6% accuracy, outperforming SesameBERT. In the HANS dataset, for heuristics labeled Entailment, both models performed well, assigning correct labels almost 100% of the time. For heuristics labeled Non-entailment, BERT performed poorly in all three cases, indicating it relied on heuristics rather than inference rules. SesameBERT performed significantly better than BERT in the "Lexical overlap" case. This suggests Gaussian blurring helps prevent models from adopting shallow heuristics. While SesameBERT performed poorly on "Subsequence" and "Constituent" heuristics, these may be hierarchical cases of lexical overlap.

SesameBERT, a fine-tuning approach based on BERT, aims to improve self-attention network performance by identifying high-quality attention output layers, extracting information via Squeeze and Excitation, and capturing local contexts with Gaussian blurring. Experiments on GLUE datasets showed SesameBERT outperformed BERT. Analysis of layer weight distributions and Gaussian blurring approaches provided insights. The HANS dataset confirmed SesameBERT's ability to learn intended information rather than relying on shallow heuristics, with lexical overlap heuristics being a notable advantage over BERT. SesameBERT can help prevent models from adopting shallow heuristics.

Fine-tuning with pre-trained models has achieved exceptional results for many language tasks. BERT, a self-attention network model, has performed well in stacking layers across diverse language-understanding benchmarks. However, BERT ignores information between layers during fine-tuning for many downstream tasks. Although self-attention networks capture global dependencies, emphasizing local contexts needs improvement.

This paper proposes SesameBERT, a generalized fine-tuning method that:
1.  Enables global information extraction among all layers through Squeeze and Excitation.
2.  Enriches local information by capturing neighboring contexts via Gaussian blurring.

The effectiveness of SesameBERT was demonstrated on the HANS dataset, used to determine if models adopt shallow heuristics instead of learning underlying generalizations. Experiments revealed that SesameBERT outperformed BERT on the GLUE benchmark and the HANS evaluation set.

In natural language processing (NLP), unsupervised pre-trained models involve a two-step framework: pretraining and fine-tuning. Pretraining trains an encoder neural network model on large-scale unlabeled data to learn word embeddings. Parameters are then fine-tuned with labeled data for downstream tasks.

Traditionally, word embeddings are vector representations learned from unstructured textual data. Each word has an independent vector, ignoring morphological similarities. Contextualized word representation techniques (e.g., Peters et al., 2018; Devlin et al., 2019) have been developed, proving more effective than conventional word-embedding techniques that extract only local semantic information. Pre-trained contextual representations learn sentence-level information from sentence encoders, generating multiple word embeddings for a word. Methods like BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), OpenAI GPT (Radford et al., 2018), and ELMo (Peters et al., 2018) have gained significant attention in NLP, achieving high accuracy in GLUE tasks. BERT, using the Transformer encoder architecture, leads in performance on the GLUE benchmark, suggesting self-attention's effectiveness in extracting latent meanings from sentence embeddings.

This study aims to improve contextualized word embeddings, the output of encoder layers fed into a classifier. The pretraining stage of BERT was used. During fine-tuning, a new architecture combining Squeeze and Excitation with Gaussian blurring and symmetrically SAME padding (SESAME) was introduced.

The developers of BERT presented several options for its use, but it was unclear whether selective layer approaches involved information from all layers. Investigations into relationships between layers revealed that the Squeeze and Excitation method (Hu et al., 2018) is crucial for focusing on information between layer weights. This method recalibrates features, improving representation quality by selectively emphasizing informative features and suppressing redundant ones.

The self-attention mechanism allows a word to analyze other words in an input sequence, leading to more accurate encoding. Its main benefit is capturing global dependencies. To focus on local contexts, Gaussian blurring was employed. A Gaussian matrix was created and convolved with a fixed window size for sentence embedding. Convolution helps a word focus on its importance and its relationships with neighboring words. This allows each word to maintain both global and local dependencies.

Multihead attention splits Q, K, and V into h subspaces of size d/h. In each subspace, the output oh_i is computed as Attention(qh_i, Kh)Vh, where oh_i is in R^d_h.

To capture local dependencies, a fixed window size k is used to create a Gaussian blur g R^k:
g(x; s, k) = exp(-(x -k/2)^2 / (2s^2))
where s is the standard deviation.

The attention output Oh is restricted to a local scope of size k centered at position i and dimension j:

eOh_i,j = ^Oh_i,j,: * g

eOh = Oh *g
where * denotes convolution.

HANS dataset heuristics:
Lexical overlap: Assume that a premise entails all hypotheses constructed from words in the premise. Example: The docter was paid by the actor. WRONG The doctor paid the actor.
Subsequence: Assume that a premise entails all of its contiguous subsequences. Example: The doctor near the actor danced. WRONG The actor danced.
Constituent: Assume that a premise entails all complete subtrees in its parse tree. Example: If the artist slept, the actor ran. WRONG The artist slept.

Object recognition models can be misled by contextual heuristics. For example, in Natural Language Inference (NLI), models may predict a label that contradicts the input if the word "not" is present, due to its common association with contradiction in training sets. To address this, SesameBERT was made robust against all training sets. Experiments used HANS datasets to identify structural heuristics that lead to errors.

METHODS

BERT, the encoder architecture of a multilayer Transformer, features improvements. An encoder consists of L layers, each with a multihead self-attention layer and a feed-forward network. The multihead mechanism uses scaled dot product attention, formulated by querying a dictionary entry with key-value pairs. Self-attention input comprises query Q Rlxd, key K Rlxd, and value V Rlxd, where l is sentence length and d is embedding dimension. For subsequent layers, Q, K, and V are outputs of the previous layer. Scaled dot product attention is defined as:

Attention(Q, K, V ) = softmax(QKT / d) * V (1)

The output is the product of attention weights A and vector v, where A = softmax(QKT / d) Rlxl. Attention weights Ai,j indicate the importance of the i-th key-value pair relative to the j-th query for generating the output. During fine-tuning, the output encoder layer from a pretrained BERT model creates contextualized word embeddings, which are then fed into the model. While various methods exist for extracting contextualized embeddings from different layers, improvements are possible. Squeeze and Excitation was used to address this.

SQUEEZE AND EXCITATION

This study proposes applying Squeeze and Excitation to the output of the encoder layer. The number of channels is equivalent to the number of layers, allowing interchangeable use of these terms.

Let U:,:,k be the output of the k-th encoder layer (1 <= k <= n). To gather global information across layers before classification, all encoder layer outputs are concatenated to form feature maps U Rlxdxn. In the squeeze step, global average pooling on the k-th layer extracts global spatial information into a layer descriptor. The k-th layer's squeeze function output is Z:,:,k:

Z:,:,k = fsq(Uk) = (1 / (l x d)) * S(i=1 to l) S(j=1 to d) Ui,j,k (2)

The figure illustrates extracting outputs from each encoder layer, concatenating them into a tensor U. Squeeze fsq(U) and Excitation fex(fsq(U)) are then applied to obtain output layer weights. Finally, a weighted average of all layers is fed into the classifier. In this work, n = 12 attention layers were used.

In the excitation step, layer-wise dependencies are fully captured. This method uses the layer-wise output of the squeeze operation fsq to modulate interdependencies of all layers. Excitation is a gating mechanism with a sigmoid activation function and two fully connected layers. Let W1 and W2 be the weights of the first and second fully connected layers, respectively, and let r be the bottleneck in layer excitation encoding layer-wise dependencies. Thus, W1 Rnxn/r, and W2 Rn/rxn. The excitation function fex is:

s = fex(z) = s(ReLU(z, W1), W2) (3)

where z is the vector squeezed from tensor Z.

Finally, Z:,:,k is rescaled by multiplying it by sk. The rescaled output is denoted euk. The scaling function fscale is defined as:

euk = fscale(sk, U:,:,k) (4)

All rescaled outputs from all encoder layers are concatenated to form rescaled feature maps eu. The architecture is shown in Figure 1. Layers are then extracted from rescaled feature maps, or a weighted average layer euavg is calculated:

euavg = (S(k=1 to n) fscale(sk, U:,:,k)) / (S(k=1 to n) sk) (5)

EVALUATION STRATEGIES, EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS & DISCUSSION
We evaluate learned representations using them as features for a linear classifier on novel supervised tasks. This transfer learning evaluation is also performed in a low-resource setting. Individual word representations are evaluated using standard benchmarks. Transfer tasks and evaluation frameworks are borrowed from Conneau et al. (2017).

EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS & DISCUSSION
Logistic regression results on 10 supervised transfer tasks using fixed-length sentence representations are presented. Performance ablations are shown when adding more tasks and increasing GRU hidden units. Adding tasks improves transfer performance. Increasing encoder capacity also improves transfer performance. Gains of 1.1-2.0% are observed on sentiment classification tasks over Infersent. Substantial gains are achieved on TREC, outperforming Infersent and a CNN-LSTM. Similar gains are seen on paraphrase identification, narrowing the gap with supervised approaches. Adding constituency parsing improves performance on sentence relatedness and entailment.

An MLP trained on fixed sentence representations outperforms complex supervised approaches with attention mechanisms, even on a large dataset. With a small fraction of training data, our approach outperforms Siamese and Multi-Perspective CNN, and the Deconv LVM model in a low-resource setting.

Learned word embeddings are competitive with GloVe, word2vec, and fasttext on standard benchmarks, despite learning them from scratch.

Sentence representations are probed to determine if sentence characteristics and syntactic properties can be inferred. Syntactic properties are better encoded with multi-lingual NMT and parsing. Representations learned from NLI encode syntax, but this signal is not amplified in the multi-task framework. Sentence characteristics like length and word order are better encoded with parsing.

Sentence representations outperform skip-thoughts and are on par with Infersent for image-caption retrieval.

Train a logistic regression classifier with 10-fold cross validation to tune the L2 weight penalty. The evaluation metric is classification accuracy.

PARAPHRASE IDENTIFICATION
Evaluate on pairwise text classification tasks such as paraphrase identification on the Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus (MRPC) corpus. This is a binary classification problem to identify if two sentences are paraphrases of each other. The evaluation metrics are classification accuracy and F1.

ENTAILMENT AND SEMANTIC RELATEDNESS
Evaluate on the SICK relatedness (SICK-R) task where a linear model is trained to output a score from 1 to 5 indicating the relatedness of two sentences. Also evaluate using the entailment labels in the same dataset (SICK-E), which is a binary classification problem. The evaluation metric for SICK-R is Pearson correlation and classification accuracy for SICK-E.

SEMANTIC TEXTUAL SIMILARITY
Measure the relatedness of two sentences using only the cosine similarity between their representations. Use the similarity textual similarity (STS) benchmark tasks from 2012-2016 (STS12, STS13, STS14, STS15, STS16, STSB). The STS dataset contains sentences from a diverse set of data sources. The evaluation criterion is Pearson correlation.

IMAGE-CAPTION RETRIEVAL
Image-caption retrieval is a ranking task wherein images are retrieved and ranked based on a textual description and vice-versa. Use 113k training images from MSCOCO with 5k images for validation and 5k for testing. Image features are extracted using a pre-trained 110 layer ResNet. The evaluation criterion is Recall@K and the median K across 5 different splits of the data.

QUORA DUPLICATE QUESTION CLASSIFICATION
Evaluate on the Quora duplicate question dataset. The task is to correctly identify question pairs that are duplicates of one another, formulated as a binary classification problem. Use the same data splits as in Wang et al. (2017). Train a 4 layer MLP with 1024 hidden units, with a dropout rate of 0.5 after every hidden layer. The evaluation criterion is classification accuracy. Create a low-resource setting by reducing the number of training examples between 1,000 and 25,000 using the same splits as Shen et al. (2017).

SENTENCE CHARACTERISTICS & SYNTAX
Consider six different classification tasks to predict sentence characteristics such as length, word content, word order, or syntactic properties such as active/passive, tense, and the top syntactic sequence (TSS) from the parse tree of a sentence. The sentence characteristic tasks are set up as described in Adi et al. (2016). The length task is an 8-way classification problem where sentence lengths are binned into 8 ranges. The content task is a binary classification problem that takes a concatenation of a sentence representation u Rk and a word representation w Rd to determine if the word is contained in the sentence. The order task is an extension of the content task where a concatenation of the sentence representation and word representations of two words in a sentence is used to determine if the first word occurs before or after the second. Use a random subset of the 1-billion-word dataset for these experiments that were not used to train multi-task representations.
The syntactic properties tasks are set up as described in Shi et al. (2016). The passive and tense tasks are binary classification problems given a sentence's representation. The passive task objective is to determine if a sentence is written in active/passive voice. The tense task objective is to determine if the sentence is in the past tense or not. The top syntactic sequence (TSS) is a 20-way classification problem with 19 most frequent top syntactic sequences and 1 miscellaneous class. Use the same dataset as the authors but different training, validation, and test splits.

ABSTRACT
Recent natural language processing (NLP) success stems from distributed word representations trained unsupervised on large text corpora, serving as general-purpose word features. Extending this to sentence representations, however, remains an open problem. Previous work explored unsupervised and supervised techniques with diverse objectives for learning general-purpose fixed-length sentence representations. This work introduces a simple, effective multi-task learning (MTL) framework for sentence representations, combining inductive biases from diverse training objectives within a single model. The model is trained on over 100 million sentences across multiple data sources with multiple training objectives. Extensive experiments show that sharing a single recurrent sentence encoder across weakly related tasks consistently improves performance over prior methods. Our learned general-purpose representations yield substantial improvements in transfer learning and low-resource settings.

1 INTRODUCTION
Transfer learning has driven recent successes in computer vision and NLP. Computer vision tasks like image captioning and visual question answering utilize CNNs pretrained on ImageNet to extract image representations. Similarly, NLP tasks like reading comprehension and sequence labeling benefit from pretrained word embeddings, either fine-tuned or held fixed. Many neural NLP systems initialize with pretrained word embeddings but learn context-specific word representations from scratch using supervised signals. However, learning these representations reliably from scratch is not always feasible, especially in low-resource settings, where general-purpose sentence representations are believed to be beneficial.

Recent work has addressed this by learning general-purpose sentence representations. However, a clear consensus on the optimal training objective or methodology for this goal is still lacking.

Understanding the inductive biases of distinct neural models is crucial for advancing representation learning. Studies show that neural machine translation (NMT) systems capture morphology and some syntactic properties. Sequence-to-sequence parsers more strongly encode source language syntax. Furthermore, research probes representations from sequence autoencoders, word embedding averages, and skip-thought vectors using an MLP classifier to investigate the encoding of sentence characteristics such as length, word content, and word order.

To generalize across diverse tasks, representations must encode multiple aspects of a sentence. Neural approaches like skip-thoughts, machine translation, natural language inference, and constituency parsing likely possess different inductive biases. Our work leverages this in a simple one-to-many MTL framework, where a single recurrent sentence encoder is shared across multiple tasks. We hypothesize that sentence representations trained on a sufficiently large number of weakly related tasks will generalize better to novel tasks unseen during training, as this process encodes the inductive biases of multiple models. This hypothesis is supported by theoretical work. While our objective is learning fixed-length distributed sentence representations, encoding the entire "meaning" of a sentence into a fixed-length vector is not always practical.

CONCLUSION & FUTURE WORK
We present a multi-task framework for learning general-purpose fixed-length sentence representations. Our primary motivation is to encapsulate the inductive biases of several diverse training signals used to learn sentence representations into a single model. Our multi-task framework includes a combination of sequence-to-sequence tasks such as multi-lingual NMT, constituency parsing and skip-thought vectors as well as a classification task - natural language inference. We demonstrate that the learned representations yield competitive or superior results to previous general-purpose sentence representation methods. We also observe that this approach produces good word embeddings.

Our work aims at learning fixed-length distributed sentence representations, capturing some of their characteristics for various tasks. The primary contribution is combining diverse sentence-representation learning objectives into a single multi-task framework. This is the first large-scale reusable sentence representation model by combining multi-lingual NMT, natural language inference, constituency parsing, and skip-thought vectors. Representations learned this way improve performance on novel tasks not used in training. These representations facilitate low-resource learning, achieving comparable performance to models trained from scratch with only 6% of the available training set on the Quora duplicate question dataset.

RELATED WORK
Learning distributed representations of phrases and sentences has a long history. Early work includes additive and multiplicative linear composition functions of word representations (Mitchell & Lapata, 2008) and combining symbolic and distributed word representations using tensor products (Clark & Pulman, 2007). Advances in learning word embeddings (Mikolov et al., 2013; Pennington et al., 2014) and deep learning have enabled learning complex non-linear composition functions of word embeddings using convolutional or recurrent neural networks (RNNs). The representation of the last element in a sequence from an RNN is typically assumed to summarize the sentence. Most supervised NLP work focuses on task-specific sentence representations rather than general-purpose ones.

Skip-thought vectors (Kiros et al., 2015), an extension of skip-gram for sentences, learn reusable representations from weakly labeled data but are time-consuming to train. Faster alternatives include sequential denoising autoencoders and shallow log-linear models (Hill et al., 2016). Simple word embedding averages have shown comparable performance to more complex models like skip-thoughts (Arora et al., 2016). A supervised approach using natural language inference data outperforms previous methods on transfer learning benchmarks (Conneau et al., 2017). Transfer learning performance refers to evaluating sentence representations on tasks unseen during training. Representations learned by NMT systems also generalize well to other tasks (McCann et al., 2017), but their attention mechanism prevents learning a single fixed-length vector representation. Their bi-attentive classification network composes information from all hidden states for improvements. Discourse-based objectives can also learn good sentence representations (Jernite et al., 2017; Nie et al., 2017).

Our work is most similar to Luong et al. (2015), who trained a many-to-many sequence-to-sequence model on diverse weakly related tasks. Key differences are their use of an attention mechanism, preventing a fixed-length vector representation, and their focus on improving performance on the same tasks used for training, rather than learning reusable representations that transfer elsewhere.

We provide a fine-grained analysis of how different tasks contribute to encoding information signals in our representations, following Shi et al. (2016) and Adi et al. (2016). Hashimoto et al. (2016) also presented a multi-task framework for textual entailment.

5.2 Task transfer
We report in Table 4 transfer tasks results for different architectures trained in different ways. We group models by the nature of the data on which they were trained. The first group corresponds to models trained with unsupervised unordered sentences. This includes bag-of-words models such as word2vec-SkipGram, the Unigram-TFIDF model, the Paragraph Vector model (Le and Mikolov, 2014), the Sequential Denoising Auto-Encoder (SDAE) (Hill et al., 2016) and the SIF model (Arora et al., 2017), all trained on the Toronto book corpus (Zhu et al., 2015). The second group consists of models trained with unsupervised ordered sentences such as FastSent and SkipThought (also trained on the Toronto book corpus). We also include the FastSent variant "FastSent+AE" and the SkipThought-LN version that uses layer normalization. We report results from models trained on supervised data in the third group, and also report some results of supervised methods trained directly on each task for comparison with transfer learning approaches.

The BiLSTM-max model trained on SNLI outperforms SkipThought vectors on MR, CR, MPQA, SST, MRPC-accuracy, SICK-R, SICK-E, and STS14. It also performs better than SkipThought-LN on MR, CR, and MPQA, except for the SUBJ dataset. Cosine metrics in the BiLSTM-max embedding space are more semantically informative than in SkipThought embedding space, with a Pearson score of 0.68 compared to 0.29 and 0.44 for ST and ST-LN on STS14. This is attributed to the SNLI matching method incorporating distance notions during training.

Models trained on SNLI yield superior results to those trained on COCO, dictionary definitions, NMT, PPDB, and SST. SST is smaller than NLI. The representations produced are higher-quality features for classification and similarity tasks. The natural language inference task constrains the model to encode semantic information, which is generally discriminative and informative for NLI.

A transfer learning approach achieves better results than state-of-the-art on the SICK task, considered an out-of-domain version of SNLI. A Pearson score of 0.885 is obtained on SICK-R, surpassing the previous 0.868. Test accuracy on SICK-E reaches 86.3%, exceeding the previous 84.5%. Transfer learning approaches on SICK-E that fine-tuned an LSTM trained on SNLI achieved 80.8% accuracy. The hypothesis is that pre-trained embeddings already contain in-domain information, and learning only the classifier limits parameters for small out-of-domain tasks.

For the COCO image-caption retrieval task, SkipThought vectors with ResNet features and increased training data improve from 33.8 to 37.9 (caption retrieval R@1) and from 25.9 to 30.6 (image retrieval R@1). The BiLSTM-max approach further improves these to 42.4 (caption retrieval) and 33.2 (image retrieval). These results are comparable to methods that directly learned sentence encoding on the task without transfer. This suggests pre-trained representations like ResNet image features and the BiLSTM-max sentence embeddings achieve competitive results.

The MultiNLI corpus, a multi-genre version of SNLI with 433K sentence pairs, offers improved coverage with ten distinct genres. Training on both SNLI and MultiNLI (AllNLI) significantly boosts performance compared to training on SNLI alone, reaching AdaSent performance on CR and suggesting larger coverage aids general representation learning. On STS14, AllNLI is competitive with PPDB-based paragram-phrase embeddings, achieving a Pearson score of 0.70. Training the sentence encoder on other genres from MultiNLI does not degrade performance on caption-related transfer tasks like COCO image caption retrieval, confirming the generalization power of the embeddings.

In conclusion, models learned on NLI outperform those trained in unsupervised conditions or on other supervised tasks. A BiLSTM network with max pooling is identified as the best current universal sentence embedding model.

The model focuses consistently more on the first and last hidden states, even across hidden states. When trained, the model learns to focus on specific words that carry most of the sentence's meaning without an explicit attention mechanism. Each hidden state incorporates information from the sentence at different levels, explaining why the trained model also incorporates information from all hidden states.

Goal: Obtain general-purpose sentence embeddings useful for a broad set of tasks.

SentEval Classifier: Logistic regression fitted with Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2014), batch size 64.

Binary and multi-class classification:
Tasks include sentiment analysis (MR, SST), question-type (TREC), product reviews (CR), subjectivity/objectivity (SUBJ), and opinion polarity (MPQA).
Procedure: Generate sentence vectors and train a logistic regression on top. Linear classifiers are suitable for small datasets and transfer learning. L2 penalty tuned via grid-search on the validation set.

Dataset: SICK (SICK-E for entailment, SICK-R for semantic relatedness).
Method: Same matching methods as SNLI, Logistic Regression on joint representation.

Caption-Image retrieval:
Task: Evaluates joint image and language feature models.
Goal: Rank images by relevance to a caption (Image Retrieval), or rank captions by relevance to an image (Caption Retrieval).
Loss function: Pairwise ranking-loss Lcir(x, y) = sum_y sum_k max(0, alpha - s(V_y, U_x) + s(V_y, U_xk)) + sum_x sum_k' max(0, alpha - s(U_x, V_y) + s(U_x, V_yk')).
Parameters: alpha (margin), s (cosine similarity), U and V (learned linear transformations).
Settings: alpha = 0.2, 30 contrastive terms.
Dataset split: 113k images from COCO (5 captions each) for training, 5k for validation (following Karpathy and Fei-Fei, 2015).

Many modern NLP systems rely on word embeddings, previously trained in an unsupervised manner on large corpora, as base features. Efforts to obtain embeddings for larger chunks of text, such as sentences, have however not been so successful. Several attempts at learning unsupervised representations of sentences have not reached satisfactory enough performance to be widely adopted. In this paper, we show how universal sentence representations trained using the supervised data of the Stanford Natural Language Inference datasets can consistently outperform unsupervised methods like SkipThought vectors on a wide range of transfer tasks. Much like how computer vision uses ImageNet to obtain features, which can then be transferred to other tasks, our work tends to indicate the suitability of natural language inference for transfer learning to other NLP tasks. Our encoder is publicly available.

1 Introduction

Distributed representations of words (or word embeddings) have shown to provide useful features for various tasks in natural language processing and computer vision. While there seems to be a consensus concerning the usefulness of word embeddings and how to learn them, this is not yet clear with regard to representations that carry the meaning of a full sentence. That is, how to capture the relationships among multiple words and phrases in a single vector remains an question to be solved.

In this paper, we study the task of learning universal representations of sentences, i.e., a sentence encoder model that is trained on a large corpus and subsequently transferred to other tasks. Two questions need to be solved in order to build such an encoder, namely: what is the preferable neural network architecture; and how and on what task should such a network be trained. Following existing work on learning word embeddings, most current approaches consider learning sentence encoders in an unsupervised manner like SkipThought or FastSent. Here, we investigate whether supervised learning can be leveraged instead, taking inspiration from previous results in computer vision, where many models are pretrained on the ImageNet before being transferred. We compare sentence embeddings trained on various supervised tasks, and show that sentence embeddings generated from models trained on a natural language inference (NLI) task reach the best results in terms of transfer accuracy. We hypothesize that the suitability of NLI as a training task is caused by the fact that it is a high-level understanding task that involves reasoning about the semantic relationships within sentences. Unlike in computer vision, where convolutional neural networks are predominant, there are multiple ways to encode a sentence using neural networks. Hence, we investigate the impact of the sentence encoding architecture on representational transferability, and compare convolutional, recurrent and even simpler word composition schemes. Our experiments show that an encoder based on a bi-directional LSTM architecture with max pooling, trained on the Stanford Natural Language Inference (SNLI) dataset, yields state-of-the-art sentence embeddings compared to all existing alternative unsupervised approaches like SkipThought or FastSent, while being much faster to train. We establish this finding on a broad and diverse set of transfer tasks that measures the ability of sentence representations to capture general and useful information.

2 Related work

Transfer learning using supervised features has been successful in several computer vision applications. Striking examples include face recognition and visual question answering, where image features trained on ImageNet and word embeddings trained on large unsupervised corpora are combined. In contrast, most approaches for sentence representation learning are unsupervised, arguably because the NLP community has not yet found the best supervised task for embedding the semantics of a whole sentence. Another reason is that neural networks are very good at capturing the biases of the task on which they are trained, but can easily forget the overall information or semantics of the input data by specializing too much.

Learning on large unsupervised tasks makes specialization harder. Co-adaptation of encoders and classifiers can negatively impact generalization power of image features. A loss incorporating multiple orthogonal classifiers can counteract this effect.

Recent sentence embedding generation models range from composing word embeddings to complex neural network architectures. SkipThought vectors adapt the skip-gram model to the sentence level by encoding a sentence to predict surrounding sentences. Using these features in a linear model shows good performance on transfer tasks. Layer-norm regularization improves results.

The task on which sentence embeddings are trained significantly impacts their quality. Supervised training on machine translation data, dictionary definitions, and image captioning data yielded lower results compared to the unsupervised Skip-Thought approach.

Recent work explored training sentence encoders on the SNLI corpus and applying them to the SICK corpus using multi-task learning or pretraining. Results were inconclusive and did not reach the level of simpler approaches that directly learn a classifier on top of unsupervised sentence embeddings. This work is the first attempt to fully exploit the SNLI corpus for building generic sentence encoders. Experiments show consistent outperformance of unsupervised approaches, even with less human-annotated data.

This work combines two research directions: using the NLI task to train universal sentence encoding models with the SNLI task, and investigating various sentence encoder architectures including LSTMs, GRUs with mean and max-pooling, self-attentive networks, and hierarchical convolutional networks.

The Natural Language Inference (NLI) task involves the SNLI dataset, comprising 570k human-generated English sentence pairs labeled as entailment, contradiction, or neutral. This dataset captures natural language inference, previously known as Recognizing Textual Entailment (RTE), and is a large, high-quality labeled resource for understanding sentence semantics. The semantic nature of NLI makes it a good candidate for supervised universal sentence embedding learning. The goal is to demonstrate that sentence encoders trained on NLI learn universally useful sentence representations.

A generic NLI training scheme uses a shared sentence encoder for premise and hypothesis inputs, followed by a 3-way softmax and fully-connected layers. Models can be trained on SNLI using sentence encoding-based models that separate sentence encoding or joint methods that use encoding of both sentences for cross-features or attention. For training a generic sentence encoder, the sentence encoding-based approach is adopted, where a shared encoder outputs representations for the premise and hypothesis. Three matching methods extract relations between the sentence vectors.

Within the same sentence, we search for "S1" to capture pairs where the discourse marker starts the sentence and connects two clauses, e.g., "Because [it was cold outside]S2, [I wore a jacket]S1." If a sentence contains only a discourse marker and S2, we assume it links to the previous sentence (IPS), labeled S1.

For some markers, we filter based on sentence order. For instance, "then" appears as "S1, then S2," unlike "because," which can also appear as "Because S2, S1." Excluding incorrectly ordered extractions enhances robustness against inaccurate dependency parses.

4.3 Training Dataset
We curated a dataset of 4,706,292 sentence pairs for 15 discourse markers. The dataset was randomly split into train/validation/test sets with 0.9, 0.05, 0.05 proportions. Although inherently unbalanced, the model effectively learns rarer classes.

5 Related Work
Current state-of-the-art models employ fully supervised learning for classification tasks or unsupervised learning. Supervised learning, trained on semantic relation tasks like SNLI and MultiNLI, yields general-purpose meaning representations. Large-scale joint supervised training has also been explored. These supervised tasks often require costly human annotations. Our discourse prediction approach extends these by training on semantic relations, using dependency patterns for automatic dataset curation.

Unsupervised learning settings include SkipThought, which learns a conditional joint probability distribution for the next sentence; ELMo, using a BiLSTM for masked word prediction; OpenAI-GPT2, predicting the next word; and BERT, using masked language modeling and next sequence prediction. While successful, fine-tuning these models on supervised datasets can improve performance.

Jernite et al. (2017) proposed a model leveraging discourse relations, manually categorizing markers based on human similarity interpretations, with the model predicting the category. Their model trains on auxiliary tasks like sentence ordering and ranking, compensating for data imbalance. Their data collection was limited to paragraphs longer than 8 sentences and sentence-initial discourse markers, yielding 1.4M sentence pairs from a larger corpus. Our model extracts a wider variety of sentence pairs, applies to shorter paragraphs, and omits auxiliary tasks.

6 Experiments
Hyperparameters were tuned on the validation set, with results reported from the test set. We used stochastic gradient descent with an initial learning rate of 0.1, annealing by a factor of 5 when validation accuracy decreased. The fixed sentence encoder model was trained for 20 epochs with early stopping. Gradient norms were clipped to 5.0. Dropout was not used in the fully connected layer for final results due to lower performance on SentEval generalization. Global mean pooling and global max pooling were experimented with, the latter performing better on generalization tasks. All reported models used a 4096 hidden state size and fit on a single Nvidia Titan X GPU.

While universal dependency grammar provides enough information to identify discourse markers and their connected statements, different discourse markers are parsed with different dependency relations. For each discourse marker of interest, we identify the appropriate dependency pattern. We excluded any pair where one of the sentences was less than 5 or more than 50 words long and any pairs where one of the sentences was more than 5 times the length of the other. Dependency parsing allows us to design our extraction method such that each S1 and S2 is interpretable as a full sentence in isolation, and the appropriate conceptual relation holds between the pair. However, occasionally we get ungrammatical sentences or the wrong pair of sentences for a relation. This incorrect extraction can happen in several ways. First, we might choose grammatical but incorrect pairs.

Ungrammatical sentences or incorrect sentence pairs can arise in several ways. First, grammatical but incorrect pairs may be chosen. Discourse markers appear in the same sentence (SS) with both S1 and S2 61% of the time, and 30% link S2 to the immediate predecessor (IPS). For non-adjacent previous sentences (NAPS - 9%) or following sentences (FS - less than 1%), the method incorrectly extracts an IPS pair. Second, not all parses are correct; for example, "Himself close his eyes." was extracted due to an incorrect parse. Finally, even with correct parses, some extracted sentences are nonsensical or ungrammatical out of context due to implicit subjects, unresolved pronouns, or marked embedded clauses. These errors are rare and can be reduced by enforcing that extracted sentences have a main verb and meet a minimum length. Overall, this method extracts high-quality sentence pairs with appropriately labeled relations.

Procedures in Extraction Validation
PTB sentences are preprocessed by limiting vocabulary size to 10,000 and tokenizing numbers. The extraction pipeline is then run on the preprocessed PTB. The same preprocessing is applied to PDTB sentences.
The gold sentence pair from the PDTB is (G1, G2), and the extracted sentence pair from the PTB is (S1, S2). The minimum of S1-G1 distance and S2-G2 distance over all gold pairs is obtained. If this distance is smaller than 0.7, the corresponding gold pair is considered an alignment for this extracted pair.
Given an aligned pair ((G1, G2), (S1, S2)), extraction quality is measured by computing the average of normalized G1-S1 and G2-S2 distance. This distance is computed for all pairs and all discourse markers.
Extraction quality is analyzed in two steps: aligning sentence pairs from the two datasets and then calculating extraction quality on each aligned pair.
In the alignment step, for each extracted pair, its distance to all pairs from PDTB is calculated using the normalized Levenshtein distance:
d(s1, s2) = Levenshtein(s1, s2) / max(len(s1), len(s2))

Implicit vs. Explicit Prediction Task Setup
For each pair of connected sentences with a labeled relation type in PDTB, the discourse relation may be explicitly marked (via a discourse relation word) or not. The task is a binary classification of whether the sentence pair appeared as explicitly or implicitly marked, given only the two sentences and no additional information. DisSent and InferSent sentence embedding models and a word vector baseline are evaluated on this task.
Patterson and Kehler (2013)'s preprocessing is followed. The dataset contains 25 sections. Sections 0 and 1 are used as the development set, sections 23 and 24 for the test set, and sections 2-22 are used for training.
This task differs from the setting in Patterson and Kehler (2013). The classifier is not allowed to access the underlying discourse relation type, and only individual sentence embeddings are provided as input features. In contrast, Patterson and Kehler (2013) used various discrete features from the PDTB dataset, including hand-annotated relation types.

Classification Performance
A confusion matrix of test set classifications is built to investigate qualitative relations among the largest set of discourse markers, the ALL marker set. This model is influenced by frequency, misclassifying infrequent discourse markers as frequent ones. Deviations from the effect of frequency appear to be semantically meaningful.
Classification errors are more common for semantically similar discourse marker pairs than expected from frequency alone. The most common confusion is when the synonymous marker although is mistakenly classified as but. Temporal relation markers before, after, and then are rarely confused for anything but each other. This confusability may reflect authors' tendency to mark temporal relation primarily when it is ambiguous.
When the model cannot rely on base rates of discourse markers, overall accuracy drops from 68% to 47%. However, the confusability is very similar, suggesting that training on unbalanced data does not greatly decrease sensitivity to non-frequency predictors.

A.7 Limitations of evaluation
Generalization tasks (sentiment, entailment, similarity) used for model comparison are narrow definitions of semantic meaning. Success on these tasks does not necessarily imply deep semantic understanding. Sentiment classification, for instance, can often rely on local structures. Text similarity can be computed using various textual distances (e.g., Levenshtein).

Table 9: Ngram Bag-of-words baseline sentence embeddings performance on DisSent training task: test recall/precision for each discourse marker, and overall accuracy. Average metric is the weighted average of all classes.

A model has learned a deep semantic understanding of a sentence. Sentiment classification, for example, in many cases only requires the model to understand local structures. Text similarity can be computed with various textual distances (e.g., Levenshtein or Jaro distance) on bag-of-words, without a compositional representation of the sentence. Thus, the ability of our, and other, models to achieve high performance on these metrics may reflect a competent representation of sentence meaning; but more rigorous tests are needed to understand whether these embeddings capture sentence meaning in general.

Single-model and ensemble results show ALBERT significantly improves state-of-the-art on GLUE, SQuAD 2.0, and RACE. ALBERT achieves a GLUE score of 89.4, SQuAD 2.0 test F1 score of 92.2, and RACE test accuracy of 89.4. The improvement on RACE is 17.4% absolute points over BERT, 7.6% over XLNet, 6.2% over RoBERTa, and 5.3% over DCMI+. The single ALBERT model achieves 86.5% accuracy, 2.4% better than the state-of-the-art ensemble model.

SQuAD and RACE benchmark results are presented for BERT-large, XLNet, RoBERTa, UPM, XLNet + SG-Net Verifier++, ALBERT (1M), ALBERT (1.5M), XLNet + SG-Net Verifier, XLNet + DAAF + Verifier, DCMN+, and ALBERT.

ALBERT-xxlarge has fewer parameters than BERT-large but is computationally more expensive. Future work includes speeding up ALBERT training and inference using sparse attention and block attention. Other research directions include hard example mining and more efficient language modeling training. Although sentence order prediction leads to better language representations, there may be other dimensions not yet captured by current self-supervised training losses that could enhance representation power.

4.7 WHAT IF WE TRAIN FOR THE SAME AMOUNT OF TIME?
Data-throughput for BERT-large is about 3.17x higher than for ALBERT-xxlarge. To compare performance with equal training time, BERT-large was trained for 400k steps (34h), while ALBERT-xxlarge was trained for 125k steps (32h). After training for similar durations, ALBERT-xxlarge outperformed BERT-large by +1.5% on average, with a difference of +5.2% on RACE.

4.8 ADDITIONAL TRAINING DATA AND DROPOUT EFFECTS
Experiments used only Wikipedia and BOOKCORPUS datasets. Incorporating additional data from XLNet and RoBERTa significantly boosted MLM accuracy and downstream task performance, except for SQuAD benchmarks, which are Wikipedia-based and negatively affected by out-of-domain training material. Even after 1M training steps, the largest models did not overfit. Removing dropout further increased model capacity and significantly improved MLM accuracy. Intermediate evaluations on ALBERT-xxlarge at 1M training steps also confirmed that removing dropout benefited downstream tasks. Empirical and theoretical evidence suggests that batch normalization combined with dropout may be detrimental in Convolutional Neural Networks. This study is the first to demonstrate that dropout can hurt performance in large Transformer-based models, although further experimentation is needed to determine if this applies to other transformer architectures.

EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
We pretrain baseline models using BOOKCORPUS and English Wikipedia, following the BERT setup. These corpora contain approximately 16GB of uncompressed text. Inputs are formatted as "[CLS] x1 [SEP] x2 [SEP]", where x1 and x2 are segments. The maximum input length is limited to 512, with input sequences shorter than 512 randomly generated with a 10% probability. A vocabulary size of 30,000 is used, tokenized with SentencePiece, similar to XLNet.

Masked inputs for MLM targets are generated using n-gram masking. The length of each n-gram mask is randomly selected with probability p(n) = 1/n / (N k=1 1/k). The maximum n-gram length is set to 3.

All model updates use a batch size of 4096 and a LAMB optimizer with a learning rate of 0.00176. Models are trained for 125,000 steps on Cloud TPU V3. The number of TPUs used ranges from 64 to 512, depending on model size. This setup applies to all BERT and ALBERT models unless specified otherwise.

EVALUATION BENCHMARKS
INTRINSIC EVALUATION
A development set is created from SQuAD and RACE development sets for monitoring training progress. Accuracies for MLM and sentence classification tasks are reported. This set is only used to check model convergence and does not influence downstream evaluation performance or model selection.

DOWNSTREAM EVALUATION
Models are evaluated on the GLUE benchmark, two versions of SQuAD, and the RACE dataset. Early stopping is performed on development sets, on which all comparisons are reported, except for final comparisons based on task leaderboards, which also include test set results. For GLUE datasets with high variance on the dev set, the median over 5 runs is reported.

OVERALL COMPARISON BETWEEN BERT AND ALBERT
ALBERT's design choices, particularly around parameter efficiency, are evaluated. ALBERT-xxlarge achieves significant improvements over BERT-large with approximately 70% of BERT-large's parameters, as shown by development set score differences on SQuAD v1.1 (+1.9%), SQuAD v2.0 (+3.1%), MNLI (+1.4%), SST-2 (+2.2%), and RACE (+8.4%).

ALBERT models exhibit higher data throughput during training due to less communication and fewer computations. ALBERT-large is about 1.7 times faster than BERT-large, while ALBERT-xxlarge is about 3 times slower than BERT-large due to its larger structure. Ablation experiments quantify the individual contribution of each design choice for ALBERT.

FACTORIZED EMBEDDING PARAMETERIZATION
The effect of changing vocabulary embedding size E is analyzed using an ALBERT-base configuration. Under a non-shared condition (BERT-style), larger embedding sizes improve performance.

ALBERT-xxlarge configurations yield negligible differences in downstream accuracy, with an identical average score. For ALBERT-style models sharing all cross-layer parameters, a 12-layer configuration is sufficient.

DOWNSTREAM EVALUATION TASKS

GLUE: GLUE comprises 9 tasks: Corpus of Linguistic Acceptability (CoLA), Stanford Sentiment Treebank (SST), Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus (MRPC), Semantic Textual Similarity Benchmark (STS), Quora Question Pairs (QQP), Multi-Genre NLI (MNLI), Question NLI (QNLI), Recognizing Textual Entailment (RTE), and Winograd NLI (WNLI). It evaluates natural language understanding capabilities. MNLI results report only the "match" condition (MNLI-m). Finetuning procedures follow prior work, reporting held-out test set performance from GLUE submissions. Task-specific modifications for WNLI and QNLI are implemented as described by prior work for test set submissions.

SQuAD: SQuAD is an extractive question answering dataset from Wikipedia where answers are context paragraph segments. The task is to predict answer spans. Evaluation is performed on SQuAD v1.1 (100,000 human-annotated question/answer pairs) and SQuAD v2.0 (adding 50,000 unanswerable questions). For SQuAD v1.1, the training procedure matches BERT. For SQuAD v2.0, models are jointly trained with a span extraction loss and an answerability prediction classifier. Both development and test set performance are reported.

RACE: RACE is a large-scale dataset for multi-choice reading comprehension from English examinations in China, with nearly 100,000 questions. Each instance has 4 candidate answers. The input to models is the concatenation of the passage, question, and each candidate answer. Representations from the "[CLS]" token are used to predict the probability of each answer. The dataset has middle school and high school domains. Models are trained on both domains and report accuracies on the development and test sets.

Our loss is similar to the sentence ordering objective where sentence embeddings are learned to determine the ordering of consecutive sentences. Unlike most prior work, our loss is defined on textual segments, not sentences. BERT uses a loss predicting if a second segment in a pair has been swapped with a segment from another document. Sentence ordering is a more challenging pretraining task and more useful for certain downstream tasks. Wang et al. (2019) also predict the order of two consecutive segments, but combine it with next sentence prediction in a three-way classification task.

THE ELEMENTS OF ALBERT
This section presents ALBERT's design decisions and quantifies comparisons against BERT configurations.

MODEL ARCHITECTURE CHOICES
The ALBERT architecture uses a transformer encoder with GELU nonlinearities, similar to BERT. Vocabulary embedding size is denoted as E, encoder layers as L, and hidden size as H. Feed-forward/filter size is 4H and the number of attention heads is H/64.

ALBERT makes three main contributions over BERT's design choices.

Factorized embedding parameterization.
In BERT, XLNet, and RoBERTa, the WordPiece embedding size E is tied with the hidden layer size H (E  H). This is suboptimal for modeling and practical reasons.

From a modeling perspective, WordPiece embeddings learn context-independent representations, while hidden-layer embeddings learn context-dependent representations. The power of BERT-like representations comes from using context. Untying E from H allows for more efficient parameter usage, as H  E.

From a practical perspective, natural language processing requires a large vocabulary size V. If E  H, increasing H increases the embedding matrix size (V x E). This can lead to billions of parameters, sparsely updated during training.

ALBERT uses a factorization of embedding parameters, decomposing them into two smaller matrices. Instead of projecting one-hot vectors directly into H, they are first projected into a lower dimensional embedding space E, and then projected to H. This reduces embedding parameters from O(V x H) to O(V x E + E x H), a significant reduction when H  E. The same E is used for all word pieces as they are more evenly distributed than whole-word embeddings, where different embedding sizes for different words are important.

Cross-layer parameter sharing.
ALBERT proposes cross-layer parameter sharing to improve parameter efficiency. Parameters can be shared in various ways, such as only sharing feed-forward network (FFN) parameters or only attention parameters. ALBERT's default decision is to share all parameters across layers. This design is compared against other strategies in our experiments.

Similar strategies were explored by Dehghani et al. (2018) (Universal Transformer) and Bai et al. (2019) (Deep Equilibrium Models) for Transformer networks. Dehghani et al. (2018) found UT outperformed a vanilla Transformer. Bai et al. (2019) showed their DQEs reached an equilibrium point where input and output embeddings of a layer remained the same. Our measurements show that ALBERT's embeddings are oscillating rather than converging.
